lessons.plain: Machine learning models learn patterns from past data so they can make predictions. Some business problems fit a standard pattern: sorting things into categories, estimating a number, predicting future values over time, or grouping similar items when nobody has labelled them. Google Cloud offers two low-code routes. BigQuery ML lets you train models with SQL inside BigQuery, Google's data warehouse. AutoML lets the platform try several model designs on your uploaded data and keep the best one. The core skill is matching the business question to the right kind of model before you choose a tool, and being able to justify that choice.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop has two years of weekly sales for each store. It wants to know next quarter's sales per store. Before reading further, which kind of model would you reach for, and why might a random shuffle of the rows be a bad idea?
lessons.teach:
The first step is to name the output the business needs. Classification predicts a category from a fixed set of labels, such as cancel or stay, or fraud or not fraud. A label is the correct answer already recorded in your historical data, so classification is supervised learning: it learns from examples that come with answers. Regression predicts a continuous number, such as delivery minutes or a house price. Forecasting also predicts a number, but the rows are ordered by time and the goal is the values that come next, such as weekly demand for the next twelve weeks. Clustering has no labels at all. An algorithm such as k-means groups rows that look similar to each other, which helps a team discover customer segments it did not know about.

Why it works: each model family fits a shape of answer, and training optimises for that shape. Feeding a yes or no target into a numeric regression produces outputs that are hard to act on.

Worked example: a subscription company asks which customers will cancel next month. Step 1: the answer is yes or no, so the problem is classification. Step 2: confirm that past customers have a recorded outcome column, cancelled or not. Step 3: if the data already lives in BigQuery and a simple model is enough, train it in BigQuery ML; if you want the platform to search more model designs, use AutoML. Step 4: evaluate on customers the model never saw during training.

Common mistake: splitting time-ordered data randomly into training and test sets. In forecasting, a random split lets the model see the future, so the reported accuracy looks better than production will be.

In a running system, a forecast validated this way will look accurate in the lab and then miss badly once stock or staffing decisions depend on it. The business question, not the tool, decides the model family.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain has two years of daily sales totals in dollars, stored in BigQuery, with one row per day. It wants the total sales for each of the next 14 days. Step 1: the output is a dollar amount per day, which is a continuous number, and the rows are ordered by date, so the problem is forecasting. Step 2: confirm that the history has a date column and a sales column. Step 3: [missing step: choose the tool and justify the choice]. Step 4: hold out the most recent 14 days as test data and evaluate on them.
choices: Use AutoML, because a platform search always beats a simple model and needs no evaluation step
Convert the sales totals into high or low labels and run a classification model
Use BigQuery ML since the data is already there; AutoML only if a wider search is needed
Train a k-means model so that days with similar sales group together
questions.why: Since the data already lives in BigQuery and a simple forecasting model may meet the goal, BigQuery ML is the natural first choice, with AutoML reserved for when a wider search of model designs is justified.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 40,000 shoppers and no labels saying which group each shopper belongs to. It wants to discover groups of shoppers who behave alike. Which model family fits?
choices: Forecasting
Classification
Regression
Clustering
questions.why: Clustering, such as k-means, groups rows that look similar without any recorded answer, which matches a request to discover unknown groups.

questions.prompt: A trucking firm has a column that records each trip as either late or on time, and a team trains a numeric regression model on that column. What is the main problem with this setup?
choices: The target is a category, so a classification model fits, and a numeric output is hard to act on as a yes or no decision
The team should cluster the trips first before predicting anything
Regression cannot use more than one input column
Regression models always need time-ordered rows
questions.why: A yes or no target is a fixed set of labels, so classification matches the shape of the answer, while a regression trained on it produces numbers that are hard to turn into a clear decision.

questions.prompt: A utility company has three years of hourly electricity readings in BigQuery and wants the daily peak demand for each of the next 30 days. Which plan is correct?
choices: Use clustering to group similar hours, then predict each group's peak
Use a forecasting model, and hold out the most recent period as test data without shuffling the rows
Use a forecasting model, and split the rows randomly into training and test sets to get more data for training
Use a classification model with labels for high and low demand days
questions.why: The output is a future numeric value from time-ordered data, so forecasting applies, and holding out the latest period keeps the test honest, whereas a random split would let the model see the future.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between classification, regression, forecasting and clustering for a new business problem, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a low-code model instead of building a custom one.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the output the business needs. If the answer is one of a fixed set of labels, like cancel or stay, it is classification and needs historical rows where the outcome is already recorded. If it is a continuous number that does not depend on time order, like delivery minutes, it is regression. If it is a number that changes over time and we need the next values, it is forecasting, and the rows must stay in time order when we split them into training and test data. If there are no labels and we want to find natural groups, it is clustering. Then I pick the tool. BigQuery ML is good when the data already sits in BigQuery and a standard model is enough. AutoML is useful when I want the platform to try more designs. The main tradeoff is control: low-code models hide much of the model design, so they may not beat a custom model on hard problems, and I need to check the results carefully before trusting them.
rubricPoints: Matches the business output (category, number, future values, or groups) to the correct model family
Notes that classification and regression need labelled historical outcomes, while clustering does not
Explains that forecasting data must keep time order when split for evaluation
Names BigQuery ML and AutoML as low-code options and says when each fits
States a real limit of low-code models, such as less control over design or harder tuning

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine trains or chooses ML models, so this objective is best learned from the teaching text and a clear mapping of business questions to model types.

lessons.plain: Feature engineering is shaping raw data into the clues a model learns from, such as turning a date into a day of the week or a text category into numbers. Feature selection is deciding which clues to keep. Think of a doctor choosing which measurements matter for a diagnosis: some readings help, some are noise, and some only become available after the diagnosis is already made. This lesson covers doing both inside BigQuery, Google's data warehouse, using SQL, so the data never has to leave the place where it lives. Getting these choices right is often the difference between a model that works in a demo and one that works on real traffic.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model must predict whether a customer will cancel a subscription next month. Which column is more dangerous to include: the customer's signup month, or a column called cancellation_reason that is filled in only after a cancellation happens? Why?
lessons.teach:
Feature engineering means turning raw table columns into the inputs a model learns from. A feature is one input column the model sees, and a label is the answer column it predicts. Feature selection means choosing which candidate features to keep. In BigQuery ML, you can write preprocessing steps inside the CREATE MODEL statement using a TRANSFORM clause. Common transforms include ML.STANDARD_SCALER, which rescales a number to a mean of zero and a standard spread of one; ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER, which turns a category into yes-or-no columns; and ML.BUCKETIZE, which groups a number into named ranges. BigQuery ML stores the transform with the model, so the same steps run automatically when you call ML.PREDICT. The scaling figures are computed from training data only, which keeps test rows from influencing the model.

Worked example: predicting whether a parcel arrives late. Start with three columns: distance_km, vehicle_type, and delivered_at. Step one: keep distance_km and scale it with ML.STANDARD_SCALER. Step two: encode vehicle_type with ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER. Step three: drop delivered_at, because it is recorded only after the outcome is known, so it would reveal the answer. Here, selection means removing a column.

Common mistake: keeping a column that is filled in after the event happens, such as a final status or a completion timestamp. The evaluation score then looks excellent, because the model is effectively cheating with information it will not have when predicting live.

In a running system, a leaked feature means predictions fail in production. The model was tuned on information that arrives too late to use, so its accuracy drops sharply once real traffic arrives.

questions.prompt: A utility wants to predict whether a household's electricity use will exceed a set limit next week. Its table has outdoor_temp_c (a number), home_type (a category such as flat or house), and is_bill_paid (filled in after the week ends). Step one: group outdoor_temp_c into named ranges with ML.BUCKETIZE, which groups a number into named ranges. Step two: encode home_type with ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER, which turns a category into yes-or-no columns. Step three is missing. Which action completes the feature selection?
choices: Keep is_bill_paid, since payment history often predicts usage.
Feed the bucket columns back through ML.BUCKETIZE to make the ranges finer.
Run ML.STANDARD_SCALER on is_bill_paid so its values have a mean of zero.
Drop is_bill_paid, because it is recorded after the week ends and would reveal the answer.
questions.why: Selection means removing a column, and is_bill_paid is filled in only after the outcome is known, so keeping it would leak the answer into training.

questions.prompt: In BigQuery ML, what is the difference between a feature and a label?
choices: A label must always be a category, while a feature must always be a number.
A feature is an input column the model sees; a label is the answer column it predicts.
A feature is the answer column; a label is an input column the model sees.
Features and labels are the same thing, named differently in each training run.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a feature as an input column the model sees and a label as the answer column it predicts.

questions.prompt: A team computes the ML.STANDARD_SCALER figures using every row in its dataset, including the test rows, before splitting the data. What is the main problem with this?
choices: Test rows influence the scaling figures, so the test score can look better than real performance.
The stored transform will refuse to run on new rows when ML.PREDICT is called.
Scaling all rows makes training run slower because the figures are larger.
The scaler turns the numbers into yes-or-no columns, which removes useful detail.
questions.why: The scaling figures should come from training data only, so test rows must not shape them, or the evaluation becomes unrealistically optimistic.

questions.prompt: A retailer trains a model to predict whether a shopper will return an item within 30 days. One feature is return_processed_at, a timestamp filled in only after a return is handled. Evaluation accuracy is 0.98, but live accuracy is poor. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The timestamp needs ML.ONE_HOT_ENCODER so each date becomes a yes-or-no column.
The bucket count is too low; raise it with ML.BUCKETIZE so the ranges are finer.
The feature leaks the outcome; drop return_processed_at during feature selection.
Too few training rows; add more history to lift the evaluation score.
questions.why: A column filled in after the event reveals the answer during training, inflating the score, and removing it is the selection step that fixes the mismatch with live traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a feature leak is, how the TRANSFORM clause in BigQuery ML helps you avoid one kind of leak, and one limit of that protection.
lessons.modelAnswer: A feature leak happens when an input column contains information that exists only because the outcome already happened, such as a completion timestamp when predicting late deliveries. The model learns from it, so test scores look strong, but at prediction time that column is unknown or empty, so live accuracy collapses. In BigQuery ML, a TRANSFORM clause stores the preprocessing steps with the model, so scaling and encoding learned from training rows are reapplied identically when ML.PREDICT runs. This prevents one common leak: computing statistics over the whole dataset, including test rows. The limit is that TRANSFORM cannot judge what a column means. If you feed it a leaking column, it will transform that column faithfully. Checking each column against the question will I know this when I predict remains the engineer's job.
rubricPoints: Defines a feature leak as information that is unavailable at prediction time.
Explains that TRANSFORM stores preprocessing so training and prediction match.
States that TRANSFORM cannot tell whether a column is legitimate.
Gives a concrete example of a leaking column.

suggested.rationale: The planned SQL lab would have the learner write and check feature transforms and column choices in SQL, which is the core practice of this objective.

lessons.plain: Once a model has been trained, the next step is asking it for answers about new cases. In BigQuery ML, a model is stored inside a data warehouse as a database object, so you can ask it for predictions using ordinary SQL, the query language for databases. You point the model at a table of rows it has never seen, such as new customers or new orders, and it returns a guess for each row: a category, a number, or a group label. Think of it like a clerk who has learned patterns from past records and now stamps each new form with an estimate, without anyone having to move the data out of the warehouse first. This lesson explains how that prediction step works, what its output looks like, and where people usually go wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model was trained last month to flag fraudulent card payments, and this morning's payments are in a table. Without any special tooling, what do you think needs to be true about that table for the model to score each payment, and what would you expect the output to contain?
lessons.teach:
A prediction here means running a trained model on new input rows to get output values. In BigQuery ML, the function that does this is named ML.PREDICT. It takes two things: a reference to a trained model, written as the dataset name plus the model name, and an input query that supplies the rows to score. The model object is held inside BigQuery, so no separate server is needed. The input rows must contain the same feature columns the model was trained on, meaning the inputs it uses to decide. The label column, the thing it learned to predict, is not needed in the input, because producing it is the whole purpose of the call.

Why it works: during training, the model learned a mapping from feature values to outcomes. Prediction simply applies that stored mapping to fresh values. The output is the input rows with new columns added. For a regression model, the new column holds a number. For a classifier, the new column is named predicted followed by the label name, and a probability for each possible class comes back as an array, so you can choose your own cutoff.

Worked example: suppose a model was trained on past orders to predict whether an order gets returned. The label column is returned, and the features are order_value and days_to_deliver. Step one, select order_id, order_value and days_to_deliver from this week's orders table. Step two, wrap that query inside ML.PREDICT together with the model reference. Step three, the result gains a predicted_returned column plus class probabilities. Step four, filter for orders whose return probability exceeds 0.8 and send them to a review queue.

Common mistake: feeding columns with different names or types than the training data, or leaving out a feature the model needs. Another frequent error is treating each output as a certainty rather than an estimate, and skipping the check that the model was evaluated on data it did not train on.

In a running pipeline, prediction is often scheduled, so a broken input query can quietly produce bad scores that still look like valid numbers. Scores are only as current as the input table they were computed from.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain trained a BigQuery ML regression model named cafe_ds.units_model to predict units_sold for each store on each day. Its training features were store_id (integer), day_of_week (integer), and rainfall_mm (float). The team wants next week's forecast. Step 1: select store_id, day_of_week and rainfall_mm from the next_week_days table. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: the result gains a predicted_units_sold column with a number for each row. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Drop rainfall_mm from the input, because weather does not affect sales forecasts
Export the step 1 result to a CSV file and load it back into BigQuery before scoring
Add the units_sold column to the input query so the model can compare its guess against actual sales
Confirm the input has the same feature column names and types the model was trained on, then wrap the query inside ML.PREDICT with the model reference
questions.why: Step 2 must ensure the input rows carry the same feature columns and types used in training, and then place that query inside ML.PREDICT with the model reference, which is what produces the predicted_units_sold column in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A parcel delivery firm has a BigQuery ML classifier that predicts whether a parcel will arrive late. Which input to ML.PREDICT is correct?
choices: The same feature columns the model was trained on, without the late-arrival label column
Only the model's internal ID, because BigQuery looks up the feature values on its own
Every column in the parcels table, since extra columns are harmless
The late-arrival label column plus the features, so the output can be checked against the truth
questions.why: ML.PREDICT applies the stored mapping from features to outcomes, so it needs the trained feature columns and does not need the label, which is what the call is meant to produce.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring query runs nightly with ML.PREDICT. The upstream source table stopped refreshing two days ago, but the query still returns rows with numeric scores and no errors. What is the main risk?
choices: The job will fail loudly on the next run, so the problem will be caught quickly
The predicted column will be empty, so downstream systems will ignore the scores
The scores look valid, yet they were computed from outdated inputs, so decisions rest on old data
BigQuery will automatically retrain the model on the stale rows and correct itself
questions.why: Scores are only as current as the input table they were computed from, and a broken or stale input can still produce plausible-looking numbers with no visible error.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking team uses a BigQuery ML classifier that predicts no_show for each appointment. ML.PREDICT returns a probability for each class as an array. How should the team use these probabilities?
choices: Accept the predicted_no_show label as a certainty and never look at the probabilities
Treat each probability as an estimate and choose their own cutoff for flagging bookings
Use the probability only when it is exactly 1.0, since anything lower is noise
Recompute the probabilities by hand from the training data before using them
questions.why: The probabilities are estimates, and the classifier returns them so the user can pick a cutoff suited to the decision being made rather than relying on a fixed label.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that once a BigQuery ML model is trained, its predictions are as good as its training score, so there is no need to look at the new inputs. Explain to them in your own words how prediction works in BigQuery ML, and name one limit or tradeoff they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: Prediction in BigQuery ML means running the stored model over new rows, using the ML.PREDICT function inside a normal SQL query. You give it the model and a query that returns rows with the same feature columns the model was trained on. It returns those rows with added prediction columns: a predicted value for a regression model, or a predicted class plus per-class probabilities for a classifier. The training score is not a guarantee. It measured performance on the data the model was built from, or on a held-out sample from the past. If the new rows look different from the training data, or a feature is missing or renamed, the scores can be wrong while still looking perfectly valid. So the tradeoff is convenience against vigilance: the model is easy to run where the data already lives, but you still need to check the inputs and watch whether predictions stay sensible over time.
rubricPoints: Prediction applies a trained model to new rows using a SQL function, without moving data out of the warehouse.
Input rows must have the same feature columns the model was trained on, and the label is not needed as input.
Output adds prediction columns, such as a predicted value for regression or a predicted class and probabilities for classification.
Training performance does not guarantee new predictions; changed inputs or missing features can yield plausible but wrong scores.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about the function's inputs, outputs and syntax, which is reference material with no listed OpsForge mission or planned engine that teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: AutoML is a service where you give a computer a table of examples that already have the right answers, tell it which column you want predicted, and it tries many different model designs and settings to find one that predicts well. You do not write the modelling code yourself. Think of it as a tester who tries dozens of recipes on your ingredients, keeps a scorecard, and hands you the best recipe along with that scorecard. It is useful when you have labeled examples but no specialist available to tune every choice by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop has two years of past orders, each marked as returned or kept. If you want a tool that predicts whether a new order will be returned, what must the training data include besides the order details, and why would a model trained without it be useless?
lessons.teach:
AutoML, short for automated machine learning, is a training service that searches for a good model on your behalf. You supply labeled data: rows where each example already carries the correct answer. The answer column is the target, also called the label. The other columns are features, the inputs the model learns from. You also set a training budget, which caps how much compute time the search may spend. The service splits your data into three parts. The training set is used to learn, the validation set is used to compare candidate models and settings, and the test set is held back and used once to report how the chosen model performs on rows it has never seen.

Why it works: the service tries many model families and settings, scores each on validation data, and keeps the best. Because the test set played no part in choosing, its score is a fair estimate of real performance.

Worked example: a table of 10,000 customers with a column churned set to yes or no. Step 1: upload the table and choose churned as the target. Step 2: set a small budget. Step 3: the service splits the rows, for example 8,000 for training, 1,000 for validation and 1,000 for testing. Step 4: it trains candidates and ranks them by a metric such as AUC, a score for how well the model separates yes from no. Step 5: the leaderboard reports an AUC of 0.88 on the test set. Step 6: you inspect the confusion matrix, a grid showing which kinds of mistakes the model makes.

Common mistake: data leakage. Suppose the table also contains a column cancellation_date that is filled in only after a customer leaves. The model will score almost perfectly because it reads the answer rather than predicting it. In production that column is empty when a prediction is needed, so the model's accuracy collapses. The consequence is a model that looks excellent in the console and fails on live traffic.

AutoML gives you a strong baseline quickly when your labeled data is clean, but it cannot tell you whether a column is legitimate. That judgement stays with you.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uploads 40,000 delivery records to AutoML and chooses late_delivery (yes or no) as the target, which is the answer column the model must predict. Step 1: upload the table and set late_delivery as the target. Step 2: set a 2-hour training budget, which caps how much compute time the search may use. Step 3: the service splits the rows into training, validation and test sets. Step 4: [MISSING]. Step 5: the service trains candidate models, ranks them by validation score, and reports the AUC (a 0 to 1 score for how well a model separates yes from no) on the held-back test set once. Which action completes the missing step 4 so that the reported test score stays a fair estimate of real performance?
choices: Raise the budget to 20 hours so that the reported test score rises.
Remove any column, such as a delivery_completed_at timestamp filled only after a delivery ends, that will be empty when predictions are needed.
Ask the service to pick the winning model using the test set, since it holds the most recent rows and so reflects current conditions.
Switch the ranking metric to plain accuracy so the leaderboard orders candidates differently.
questions.why: Columns recorded only after the outcome is known leak the answer, and checking column legitimacy is the learner's job because AutoML cannot judge it.

questions.prompt: A bakery exports a table with columns order_size, hour_of_day, weather and sold_out_by_noon (yes or no). It wants AutoML to predict sold_out_by_noon. In AutoML terms, which column is the target?
choices: hour_of_day
weather
sold_out_by_noon
order_size
questions.why: The target, also called the label, is the answer column that already holds the correct result for each row, and here that is sold_out_by_noon.

questions.prompt: A transit agency has two years of bus records and asks AutoML to predict whether a bus will run more than 5 minutes late. After training, which split should be used exactly once to report how the chosen model performs on rows it has never seen?
choices: The training set
The test set
The budget set
The validation set
questions.why: The test set is held back, played no part in choosing the model, and is used once to report performance on unseen rows, so it is the only fair source for that final score.

questions.prompt: A wind-farm team builds an AutoML model to predict whether a turbine will fail within 30 days. The console shows a near-perfect AUC. The table includes a repair_order_number column that is filled in only when a repair is logged after a failure. What is the most likely explanation and consequence?
choices: AUC is always inflated for turbine data, so the near-perfect score is normal and can be trusted.
The budget was too small, so the search stopped early; raising it will bring the score down to a realistic level.
The validation set was too large, so the model memorised it and the score is inflated.
The column leaks the answer, which is empty when live predictions are made, so real performance will be far lower than the console score.
questions.why: A column populated only after the outcome is known reveals the answer during training, so the model looks excellent but fails once that column is blank in production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose AutoML training over writing your own model code, and name one limit or tradeoff you would check before trusting the result.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would reach for AutoML when we have a clearly labeled table or set of examples, a well-defined prediction target, and want a solid baseline quickly without a specialist tuning every setting. The service handles the search over model types and settings within a budget, and it reports results on a held-back test set. The tradeoff is control: we get less say over the model's design, and we pay for the compute the search uses. Before trusting the score, I would check for leakage, meaning any input column that only gets filled in after the outcome happened. A suspiciously high score is usually a sign of that. I would also confirm the test data resembles what the model will see in production, because a good test score on the wrong kind of data tells us little.
rubricPoints: Names labeled data and a clear target as the prerequisites for AutoML training
Explains the tradeoff of less control over the model design in exchange for speed
Identifies data leakage as the main risk and how an unusually high score can reveal it
Notes that the held-back test data must resemble real production inputs

suggested.rationale: Choosing AutoML and defending the tradeoff in your own words is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Fine-tuning means taking a model that has already learned general language skills and training it a little further on your own examples, so it behaves the way your business needs. Imagine hiring an experienced writer and then giving them a week with your company's style guide and past work. They already know how to write, so they need far less practice than a beginner. Here the examples are pairs of inputs and the answers you want. The decision you must make is whether this extra training is worth doing, or whether a simpler approach such as a clearer instruction, a classic prediction model, or a few reference documents would solve the problem well enough.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a Gemini model to always reply with one label from a fixed list of ticket categories. Before any training, would you first try a clearer instruction in the prompt, or fine-tune the model on past tickets? Why?
lessons.teach:
Fine-tuning means taking a pretrained foundation model, such as a Gemini model, and training it further on your own labeled examples so its answers shift toward your task. A labeled example is one input paired with the output you want, for instance a support ticket and its correct category. BigQuery is Google Cloud's data warehouse, where your tables already live. The BigQuery route lets you prepare the examples with SQL, start a tuning job against a Gemini model without exporting the data, and call the tuned model from SQL afterwards. It works because the base model already understands language; your examples teach it your labels, format and vocabulary, so it needs far fewer examples than training from scratch.

Worked example: a retailer wants product descriptions in a fixed three-field format. Step 1: select past product rows that have an approved description, and shape each into an input text and a target output. Step 2: hold back about 10 percent as an evaluation set that training never sees. Step 3: start the tuning job on the remaining rows. Step 4: when it finishes, run the tuned model on the held-out rows and measure how often the format is correct, comparing it with the untuned base model. Step 5: only if the tuned version clearly wins on that held-out set, point the application at it.

Common mistake: tuning on noisy or inconsistent examples, or evaluating on the same rows used for training, which makes results look better than they are. Consequence in a running system: a tuned model that learned bad labels repeats them across every request, and each time the base model is upgraded the tuning and its evaluation must be checked again.

Fine-tuning is the right tool when clear instructions and reference documents cannot produce a consistent format or behaviour, and when you have enough clean labeled examples to justify the cost and upkeep.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer wants adjuster notes on car claims sorted into one of five cause codes, using the same kind of BigQuery-based fine-tuning on a Gemini model. The team follows these steps. Step 1: from the claims table, select 4,000 past notes that have a cause code approved by a senior adjuster, and shape each into an input text (the note) and a target output (the code). Step 2 is missing from their plan. Step 3: hold back 15 percent of the rows as an evaluation set that training never sees. Step 4: start the tuning job on the remaining rows. Step 5: run both the tuned model and the untuned base model on the held-out rows, and switch only if the tuned version is clearly more accurate. Which missing step fits between steps 1 and 3?
choices: Find notes that appear more than once with different cause codes, and fix or remove them so each input has one consistent label.
Raise the held-out share to 50 percent so the tuned model is judged on a larger, harder set.
Retrain the base Gemini model from random starting weights on all 4,000 rows before any tuning begins.
Export the 4,000 rows to Cloud Storage as CSV files, because tuning jobs cannot read BigQuery tables directly.
questions.why: Inconsistent labels teach the tuned model conflicting rules, so the examples must be cleaned before the split and training, which is why option three is the right missing step.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does fine-tuning a pretrained model such as Gemini mean?
choices: Further training an existing pretrained model on your own labeled examples so its answers move toward your task.
Building a new language model from random starting values using only your company's documents.
Writing a longer instruction in the prompt so the model reads your rules before each request.
Copying the base model into a second table so each team can keep its own version of it.
questions.why: The teaching text defines fine-tuning as continuing to train a pretrained foundation model on your own labeled examples, which shifts its output toward your task.

questions.prompt: A travel company needs its trip-planner replies to always come back in one fixed JSON layout. Prompt instructions alone still produce broken layouts about 40 percent of the time. The company has 8,000 clean, labeled past replies stored in BigQuery. Which choice is best justified by the teaching text?
choices: Fine-tune a Gemini model using the labeled replies in BigQuery, then evaluate it on held-out replies before switching.
Keep adding more instructions and examples to the prompt, since no training is ever needed for a format problem.
Train a new model from scratch on the 8,000 replies, since the base model cannot learn from examples at all.
Replace the language model with a rule-based template engine, because fine-tuning cannot change output format.
questions.why: Clear instructions have failed to produce a consistent format and there are enough clean labeled examples, which is exactly the case the teaching text gives for fine-tuning through BigQuery.

questions.prompt: A team tuned a model on 2,000 labeled rows and reported 95 percent accuracy, but they measured that accuracy on the same 2,000 rows used for training. What is the main problem with this result?
choices: Accuracy cannot be measured for fine-tuned models, so the team should report a different number instead.
The team should have used more training rows, because 2,000 rows is too few for any evaluation to mean anything.
The base model is too weak, so any tuned result will look good no matter how it was measured.
The score is inflated because training rows were reused for evaluation, so the tuned model is not tested on unseen examples.
questions.why: Testing on rows the model was trained on makes results look better than they are, and the fix is holding back rows that training never sees for evaluation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would fine-tune a Gemini model from BigQuery rather than use a classic BigQuery ML model or a well-written prompt, and name one limit or tradeoff of fine-tuning.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would fine-tune when the output has to follow a consistent format or domain behaviour that a good prompt cannot reliably produce, and when we already have a few thousand clean input and output pairs. If the task is a standard prediction, such as forecasting demand or classifying rows into a known set, a BigQuery ML model is cheaper and easier to explain, so I would start there. The main tradeoff is maintenance: a tuned model costs more to train and serve, needs a held-out evaluation set to prove it beats the base model, and must be re-checked whenever the underlying base model changes. Bad training labels also get baked in, so data quality matters more than the training itself.
rubricPoints: Fine-tuning means further training a pretrained model on your own labeled examples.
Choose it only when prompting or simpler models cannot meet the consistency or format need.
Classic BigQuery ML suits standard predictions and is cheaper to run and explain.
A limit is cost and upkeep, including evaluation on held-out data and re-checks after base model changes.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is justifying a low-code versus foundation-model choice in words, which explaining it to a teammate tests directly.

lessons.plain: A model catalogue is a shelf of ready-made machine learning models that other people trained, which you can look at, try out, and use without building one from scratch. Choosing from it means asking which model fits your problem, your data, your budget, and your rules. You compare a few candidates on a small set of your own real examples rather than trusting the marketing claims. The skill is matching the job to the right kind of model and being able to say clearly why you picked it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a feature that writes a two-sentence summary of each customer support ticket. They have a catalogue with dozens of models, some large and expensive, some small and cheap. Before reading anything, what would you check first to decide which one to try?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on huge amounts of general data, which can handle many tasks such as summarizing, answering questions, or describing images when you give it instructions. A prompt is the instruction and input you send to such a model. Latency is how long one request takes to return an answer. Cost per call is what you pay each time the model runs, and it usually grows with the amount of text sent in and out. An evaluation set is a set of past examples with known good answers that you hold back and use to score candidate models fairly.

Worked example. The team has 200 past tickets with human-written summaries. Step 1: state the task, which is a two-sentence summary of a ticket of up to 500 words. Step 2: shortlist two text models from the catalogue, a large one and a smaller one. Step 3: hold back 50 tickets as the evaluation set and run both models on them. Step 4: score each summary for missing facts and wrong facts. Step 5: multiply the expected 20,000 tickets a day by the per-call cost and check the response time against the target. Step 6: pick the smaller model if its quality meets the bar, because it is cheaper and faster.

Common mistake: choosing the largest model by default, or judging quality from three demo prompts. Consequence in a running system: cost and latency scale with volume, so a model that is slightly better but several times slower can break a response-time target at production traffic. If the task were instead predicting a number or category from a structured table, a low-code option such as BigQuery ML or AutoML may fit better than a foundation model.

questions.prompt: A shipping company wants a model to write a 15-word delay notice for each late parcel, about 8,000 notices an hour, with a target of 2 seconds per notice. A notice here means the text sent to the customer. Step 1: state the task as a 15-word delay notice per late parcel. Step 2: shortlist two text models. Model A costs 0.0004 per call and answers in 1.1 seconds. Model B costs 0.0021 per call and answers in 0.6 seconds. Step 3: hold back 60 past delay notices with approved wording as an evaluation set, meaning past examples with known good answers kept aside for scoring, and run both models on them. Both models meet the quality bar. Step 4 is missing from this trace. Work out the hourly spend for Model A at 8,000 notices an hour. Which result is correct?
choices: $0.32 an hour
$8,000 an hour
$3.20 an hour
$16.80 an hour
questions.why: Hourly spend is the per-call cost times the number of calls, so 8,000 multiplied by 0.0004 gives 3.20 dollars an hour.

questions.prompt: Why should the evaluation set be kept separate from the examples you used to write and adjust the instructions sent to a model?
choices: It is required before a model can appear in the catalogue
It makes the model run faster on each call
It gives a fair score, because those examples did not shape the instructions
It lowers the cost per call by shortening the input
questions.why: If you score a model on the examples you tuned your instructions against, the result flatters it, whereas held-back examples show how it handles cases it was not shaped around.

questions.prompt: A bank has a spreadsheet of 50,000 past loan applications with columns such as income, loan size and whether the loan defaulted. It wants a model that predicts default for new applications. Which approach fits best, according to the idea that structured tables with a known target often suit low-code tools?
choices: The largest foundation model available, because bigger always fits better
A foundation model with a long prompt that lists every row
A low-code option such as BigQuery ML or AutoML, since the data is a structured table with a known target
A foundation model, because any table can be turned into text and judged by eye
questions.why: Predicting a category or number from a structured table is the case where a low-code option is the more natural fit, as the teaching text notes.

questions.prompt: Model X scores about 4 percent better than Model Y on the evaluation set. However, at the expected production traffic, Model X takes 3.5 seconds per response against a target of 1.5 seconds. What is the right decision?
choices: Choose Model X and add more prompts to reduce its latency
Choose Model Y, since Model X breaks the response-time target at production traffic
Choose whichever model has the response time closer to 1.5 seconds on average across tests
Choose Model X, since quality is the main criterion
questions.why: Latency scales with volume, so a model that misses the response-time target at production traffic is rejected even if its quality is slightly higher.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a model from the catalogue for a new feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the task and the constraints: input type, expected volume, response-time target, budget per call, and data handling rules. Then I would shortlist two or three candidates that handle that input type. I would hold back a set of real past examples with known good outputs and run each candidate on them, scoring the results against a rubric such as missing facts and wrong facts. I would also estimate cost and latency at expected traffic. The tradeoff is that the evaluation set is only as good as its examples, so a small or unrepresentative set can make a weak model look strong. Also, the best quality model is often the most expensive, so I would accept a slightly lower score if the cheaper model meets the bar.
rubricPoints: Defines the task and its constraints such as volume, latency, and cost before comparing models
Compares candidates on a held-out set of real examples, not demo prompts
Accounts for per-call cost and response time at production volume
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as unrepresentative test data or quality versus cost

suggested.rationale: Choosing between candidates against stated constraints is best practised through a scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model selection yet.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a business does not need to train its own AI. Instead it can send a picture, a scanned form or a piece of text to a ready-made service run by a cloud provider and get the answer back: the text inside an image, the fields on an invoice, the objects in a photo, or the same text in another language. Think of it like hiring a specialist firm rather than training a new employee. The skill here is recognising when a pre-built service fits the problem and when it does not. This lesson covers three of these services and the kind of problem each one solves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company receives 50,000 paper receipts a month and wants the date and total on each one typed into a spreadsheet automatically. Would you build a new model trained on their receipts, or look for an existing service first? What would make you change your answer?
lessons.teach:
An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for one program to ask another program for a result over the network. A pre-trained API is one where the provider has already trained the underlying AI model on very large amounts of data, so you call it without training anything yourself. Google Cloud offers several of these, and three matter for this objective. Document AI reads business documents such as invoices, forms and identity papers and pulls out named fields. Vision analyses images. It can read text in a photo (optical character recognition, or OCR, which turns pixels of printed or handwritten letters into text), label what is in a picture, and locate objects. Translate converts text from one language to another.

Why does this work? The provider has spent far more effort on data and training than a single team usually can, so you pay per request and get good accuracy on common cases. You trade control for speed. You cannot change the model's internals, and you can only teach it your own categories if the product offers that setting.

Worked example: a clinic wants patient intake forms turned into records. Step 1: a scanned form arrives as an image file. Step 2: the application sends the file to Document AI through its API. Step 3: the service returns the recognised fields, such as name and date of birth, each with a confidence score. Step 4: the application sends any field with a low score to a person to check. Step 5: the verified fields are saved.

Common mistake: assuming a pre-trained service is accurate for your specific documents. A general invoice reader may struggle with an unusual layout, so test it on your own samples before rollout.

In a running system, every call is a network request with latency and a per-request cost, and the service can be briefly unavailable, so the application needs retries and a fallback path. Pre-trained services are quick to adopt, but their results are only as good as the match between your data and what the service was trained on.

questions.prompt: A parcel depot photographs shipping labels on staff phones and wants tracking numbers saved to its records automatically. Step 1: the phone uploads the photo to the depot's server. Step 2: the server sends the image to Vision's text-reading feature through its API. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the tracking number is saved to the parcel record. Which missing step best completes the process?
choices: The server retrains Vision on the depot's labels before every upload so the text reading improves.
The server deletes the photo immediately after step 2 to save storage, since the image is no longer needed.
The server asks Translate to convert the label text into English before saving anything.
The server receives the text Vision read with confidence scores, checks the tracking number's format, and sends unclear reads to a person before saving.
questions.why: The response carries confidence scores, so the application must check uncertain results and route them to a person before saving, which is the same verification pattern the teaching text uses for low-scoring fields.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a pre-trained API in the sense used for Google Cloud's document, image and translation services?
choices: A service where you must collect and label your own data and train a model before you can call it.
A service that runs only on your own hardware and never sends requests over a network.
A service that lets you change the model's internal weights while still using the provider's training data.
A service where the provider has already trained the underlying model, so you call it over the network without training anything yourself.
questions.why: A pre-trained API is defined by the provider having already trained the model, so the caller only sends requests and receives results.

questions.prompt: A small museum has 40,000 photos of artifacts and wants them sorted into its own catalogue categories such as pottery and textiles. A team proposes using a general image-labelling service because it is quick to adopt. What is the most important risk to test first?
choices: The general labels may not match the museum's own categories or its unusual objects, so accuracy on the museum's samples must be measured before rollout.
The service will automatically rename the files, breaking the museum's catalogue links.
Each call costs nothing, so the museum cannot estimate its total budget.
The labelling service will refuse to process photos taken with a phone camera.
questions.why: A pre-trained service is only as good as the match between the data and what it was trained on, so the museum must test its own samples against its own categories.

questions.prompt: A city council's website calls Translate in real time for every public notice shown in another language. During a short service outage, notices fail to appear for residents. Which design best handles this in a running system?
choices: Send each request again without any delay or limit until the service responds, since the outage must end.
Remove the translation feature entirely so that the page never depends on a network call.
Retry failed requests with a limit, and fall back to showing the original-language notice with a note that translation is pending.
Store only the translated text from the first request and never store the original, so a failure leaves nothing to show.
questions.why: Because every call is a network request that can be briefly unavailable, the application needs bounded retries and a fallback path that still shows residents useful content.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use Document AI, Vision or Translate instead of training your own model, and name one limit or tradeoff of using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would reach for one of these pre-trained APIs when the task is common and well defined: reading invoices or forms with Document AI, pulling text or labels from images with Vision, or translating text with Translate. The provider has already trained these models on large datasets, so we get a working result by sending requests rather than collecting data and training. That saves time and avoids needing ML specialists for a first version. The main tradeoff is control. We cannot change how the model works, and it may be less accurate on our unusual documents or images than a model trained on our own examples. So before committing I would run a sample of our real data, check the confidence scores and error rate, and decide whether the accuracy is good enough or whether we need a custom model. Each call also has a per-request cost and network latency that must be planned for.
rubricPoints: Explains that these are pre-trained models that are called through an API, not trained by the team.
Matches each service to its task: documents, images, and text translation.
States the tradeoff: less control and possibly poor fit with unusual data.
Recommends testing on real samples and checking confidence scores before relying on the service.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers choosing and calling pre-trained vendor APIs, so reading the product facts and practising the choice on your own is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Some AI jobs are better handled by a large pre-trained model that you reach over the internet than by building your own model from scratch. A foundation model is a very large model trained once on broad data, such as text, images or video, so it already knows a lot before you touch it. Google offers several of these as managed services: Gemini for text and multimodal reasoning, Imagen for generating images, and Veo for generating video. You send a request, often a written instruction called a prompt, and get an answer back. This lesson is about recognising when that route fits a business problem, and when a simpler model you train on your own table of data fits better.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants a tool that writes short product descriptions from a list of attributes such as colour, size and material. Would you train a new model on the company's own sales table, or send each request to an existing large language model? What would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach: A foundation model is a very large model trained once on broad data and then reused for many tasks. Gemini works with text and other inputs to generate and reason, Imagen generates images, and Veo generates video. Model Garden is the catalogue where these and other models are listed. Models-as-a-service means you call a model through a managed API instead of hosting it yourself, and you usually pay per request, measured in tokens (small pieces of text) processed. This works because the model has already learned language and visual patterns, so your main job is to describe the task clearly in a prompt. When the general answer is not good enough, you can add facts at request time, which is called grounding, or train the model further on your own examples, which is called tuning. Worked example: the retailer wants a two-sentence description from colour, size and material. Step one, write a prompt template with three placeholders. Step two, fill in the values for one product. Step three, send the request to Gemini through the managed API. Step four, read the reply and check it against the attributes, because the model may invent a feature. Common mistake: using a generative model to predict a number, such as next month's sales, from a large historical table. A BigQuery ML forecast or regression trained on that table is cheaper, repeatable and easier to explain. Consequence: every call adds latency and cost, and the same prompt can produce different wording, so production systems need output checks and a fallback. Choose a foundation model when the output is language, images or video and the labelled examples a custom model would need are scarce.

questions.prompt: A used-bike marketplace wants to estimate a fair resale price for each listing from its own history of 50,000 past sales, which have columns for make, model year, mileage and final sale price. The team works through these steps. Step 1: confirm the output is a single number, not language, an image or a video. Step 2: choose a BigQuery ML regression, since it is trained on the sales table in place of a hosted generative model. Step 3: train the regression with final sale price as the label and make, year and mileage as the inputs. Step 4 is missing and must be chosen next. Which step completes the workflow before the model is used on new listings?
choices: Send each new listing to Gemini and ask it to write the price in a sentence.
Pass each bike photo to Imagen so the price can be read from the picture.
Hold back a share of the past sales rows, then measure how far the predictions miss on those rows the model never saw during training.
Use grounding to add today's advertised prices to every request sent to a hosted model.
questions.why: Holding back unseen rows and measuring prediction error is the check that shows whether the trained regression is accurate enough, and the other three options either move a numeric task into a generative model or use methods that do not complete a regression workflow.

questions.prompt: A small analytics startup calls a hosted language model through a managed API rather than running the model on its own servers. Which quantity does the provider most typically bill for in this arrangement?
choices: The tokens, meaning small pieces of text, that are processed per request
The number of distinct users who log in to the startup's dashboard
The gigabytes of training data the startup uploads once
The number of servers the startup rents each month
questions.why: Models-as-a-service are usually billed per request by the tokens processed, so the cost depends on the text handled in each call rather than on servers, users or one-off uploads.

questions.prompt: A design agency needs a background scene generated for each of 400 product photos, with no labelled examples of the agency's own style available. Which choice best fits the guidance for picking a foundation model?
choices: Train a BigQuery ML classifier on the photo file names
Hand-write a rule table that maps each product colour to a background
Use Imagen, because the output is an image and labelled examples for a custom model are scarce
Use a linear regression on the photos' pixel averages
questions.why: The output is an image and the labelled examples a custom model would need are scarce, which is the situation where the text recommends a foundation model such as Imagen.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants to predict next quarter's parcel volume for each warehouse from four years of daily counts stored in a table. A team member proposes sending the table to Gemini and asking it to state the next quarter's number. What is the main problem with this proposal?
choices: Tokens cannot be counted on numbers, so the bill would be impossible to estimate.
Gemini cannot accept any table data, so the request would fail outright.
A generative model is a costly, less repeatable way to produce a number, whereas a BigQuery ML forecast trained on the table is cheaper, repeatable and easier to explain.
Imagen must be used for any tabular data, so Gemini is the wrong product.
questions.why: The text names predicting a number from a large historical table with a generative model as the common mistake, and a BigQuery ML forecast is the cheaper, repeatable alternative; the other options contain false claims about Gemini, Imagen or tokens.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between sending a business problem to a foundation model such as Gemini and building a low-code model in BigQuery ML or AutoML. Name one limit or tradeoff of the foundation-model route.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the shape of the output. If the answer is free-form language, an image or a video, a foundation model is usually the right first choice, because I can get a working result by writing a clear prompt and calling a managed model without collecting a large labelled dataset. If the answer is a number or a category that comes from rows in a table, such as a demand forecast or a churn flag, I would look at BigQuery ML or AutoML first, since they train on that data directly and produce results that are easier to measure and explain. The main tradeoff of the foundation-model route is that each call costs money and adds latency, and the wording can vary between calls. So I would add output checks against the source facts and a fallback path before I put it into production, and I would say that clearly to the team.
rubricPoints: States that foundation models suit language, image or video outputs and are reached through managed APIs
Says low-code BigQuery ML or AutoML suits structured tabular prediction with labelled data
Justifies the choice from the form of the output and the data available
Names a concrete limit of the foundation-model route, such as cost, latency or variable output
Mentions a check or fallback needed for generative output in production

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a foundation model and a low-code model is best practised by reasoning through a realistic business scenario with trade-offs.

lessons.plain: When a team builds an app on a large AI model, two things drive both the bill and the speed: how much text goes in and comes out, and how the app behaves when the service is busy or down. Optimizing means making those choices deliberately: send fewer words where you can, pick a model sized to the task, reuse work you have already paid for, and plan what happens when a request fails. Think of a delivery company that pays per mile. Shorter routes, the right size of van for each job, and a backup plan for rush hour all matter. This objective asks you to weigh cost, speed, and reliability against each other rather than optimizing just one.
lessons.guessPrompt: An app sends a 5,000-word company manual with every customer question so the model can answer. The manual never changes. Which single change would most likely cut both cost and response time, and why?
lessons.teach:
Cost, latency and availability are three separate dials. Cost is what you pay for each request. Latency is how long a user waits for an answer. Availability is the share of requests that succeed, especially when the service is busy or failing.

Gemini-based applications are usually billed by tokens. A token is a small piece of text, roughly a fragment of a word. Input tokens are what you send, including instructions and any documents. Output tokens are what the model writes back. Generating output usually takes longer than reading input, so long answers add delay as well as cost.

Worked example. A support assistant receives 10,000 questions a day, and each request includes a 4,000-token policy document. Step 1: input volume is 10,000 times 4,000, which is 40 million input tokens a day. Step 2: the team sends only the three relevant paragraphs, about 600 tokens, cutting input to 6 million. Step 3: the policy text repeats in every request, so the team uses context caching, which stores a repeated prefix so later requests reuse it at a reduced rate. Step 4: answers are capped at 150 output tokens, since users only need a short reply. Each lever is measured separately.

Latency has another factor, the time to first token, which is the wait before any text appears. Streaming shows text as it is generated, so the app feels faster even when total time is unchanged.

Availability depends on handling failures. Overloaded services return errors. Retrying with exponential backoff means waiting progressively longer between attempts, with some random jitter so many clients do not retry at the same moment. For non-urgent work such as nightly summaries, batch processing trades speed for lower cost. For critical paths, a fallback to a smaller model or a cached answer keeps the feature working.

A common mistake is defaulting to the largest model and never tuning anything. A large model may be overkill for short classification or extraction, and it costs more on every call.

In a running system, unbounded prompts and unlimited retries can turn a traffic spike into a bill spike and a cascade of timeouts. Set token budgets, timeouts and retry limits before launch, and track token counts per request.

questions.prompt: A language-learning app grades 3,000 student essays each night. Each request includes a 1,200-token scoring rubric. Step 1: the team places the rubric in a cached prefix so repeated copies are billed at a reduced rate. Step 2: because no user is waiting on a screen, the grading job moves to batch processing to lower cost. Step 3 is missing. During the run, some requests return overload errors, and the team needs a rule for retrying them. Which choice completes the plan?
choices: Switch every essay to the largest model so that the overload errors stop appearing.
Turn on streaming for the nightly job so that the errors show up earlier and can be fixed.
Retry failed requests with exponential backoff and random jitter, and stop after a set retry limit.
Retry each failed request immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds, so the night finishes sooner.
questions.why: Exponential backoff with jitter spaces retries out progressively and randomly, and a retry limit keeps failures from turning into unbounded traffic, which is the availability step the plan lacks.

questions.prompt: In the sense used for Gemini-based applications, what does availability measure?
choices: The total number of input tokens a feature sends in one day.
How long a user waits before the first word of an answer appears.
The share of requests that succeed, especially when the service is busy or failing.
The price charged for each output token the model writes back.
questions.why: Availability is defined in the teaching text as the share of requests that succeed, particularly under load or failure, which is distinct from cost and latency.

questions.prompt: A team runs a sentiment tagger that labels 80,000 product reviews a day as positive, negative, or neutral. It calls the largest available model for every review and the monthly bill is high. Which first step best fits the teaching text?
choices: Remove the output cap so the model can explain each label in full.
Keep the largest model and add a longer instruction so the labels are more consistent.
Test a smaller model on a sample of reviews, measure its accuracy, and cap the output to the label itself.
Move the tagging to a streaming interface so users see labels appear sooner.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that the largest model may be overkill for short classification and costs more on every call, so trying a smaller model and capping output tokens is the tuning step it recommends.

questions.prompt: A feature sends a 5,000-token document with every request, has no limit on output length, and retries failed calls without any cap. During a traffic spike, the bill and the timeouts both rise sharply. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Output tokens are always free, so the spike came entirely from input tokens.
Unbounded prompts and unlimited retries multiply the work per request, so cost and timeouts grow together.
Streaming was not enabled, so every request waited for the full answer before returning.
The model's training data was too large, so each token became more expensive.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that unbounded prompts and unlimited retries can turn a traffic spike into both a bill spike and a cascade of timeouts, which is what the scenario describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce the cost and latency of a Gemini-powered feature without making it less reliable, and name one tradeoff your changes introduce.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by measuring where tokens go: input size per request, output length, and how often the same context repeats. Then I would trim the input to only the relevant passages, cap output length to what users actually need, and reuse any repeated prefix through caching so it is not paid for in full each time. For latency, I would stream responses so users see text sooner. For availability, I would add retries with exponential backoff and jitter, plus a timeout and a fallback to a smaller model or a canned response when the main call keeps failing. The tradeoff is that aggressive trimming can remove context the model needed, so I would check answer quality against a fixed test set before and after each change.
rubricPoints: Identifies cost drivers: input tokens, output tokens, and repeated context
Names a latency lever such as shorter output or streaming, and explains time to first token or perceived speed
Explains availability measures such as retries with backoff and jitter, timeouts, and fallbacks
States a real tradeoff, such as lower quality from trimmed context or a weaker fallback model

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model in fictional credits would let the learner compare token and model choices against cost and latency targets, which reasoning alone does not practise well.

lessons.plain: Before a computer can learn from data, the data has to be arranged so people and programs can find it, understand it, and reuse the same version later. Data usually comes in three shapes. Tabular data is a spreadsheet-like table, where rows are examples and columns are measurements. Text is words in documents or messages. Images are picture files. Each shape needs different organizing, but the goals are the same: know what each piece means, keep a stable copy, look at the data before trusting it, and prepare it for live use the same way you prepared it for training. Think of a well-kept kitchen, with ingredients labeled, sorted, and measured the same way every time you cook.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 500,000 product photos in one folder and a spreadsheet that says which category each photo belongs to. Before you train anything, what would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach: A schema is the agreed description of a table: its column names, their types, and what each column means. A feature is an input column the model uses. A label (also called the target) is the answer the model learns to predict. A split divides the data into a training set (the model learns from it), a validation set (you compare choices with it), and a test set (you check the final result once). Tabular data should have one row per example, a stable identifier, and consistent column types. Text should be stored one document per row or file, with the raw text kept unchanged, any cleaned version saved separately, and the language and encoding recorded. Images should be stored as files in one location, with a manifest table that lists each file path, its label, and its split. Exploring means looking before modeling: summary statistics, missing-value counts, how many examples each label has, and a sample of rows, documents, or pictures. Why this works: a fixed snapshot and fixed splits let two experiments be compared honestly, and rerunning gives the same result. Worked example: a table of 10,000 delivery trips with columns distance, duration, and a label late (yes or no). Step 1: check the schema, so distance is a number and late is yes or no. Step 2: count missing durations, which turns out to be 120 rows. Step 3: choose a rule for those rows and write it down. Step 4: split by trip date, with the oldest 80 percent for training, the next 10 percent for validation, and the newest 10 percent for test. Step 5: save this as a dated, versioned snapshot. Common mistake: computing an average or scaling values over the full table before splitting, so information from the test set leaks into training. Consequence: the offline score looks strong, but in production the model underperforms because live inputs are not prepared the same way as training inputs, which is called training-serving skew. Keep the split and cleaning rules fixed and recorded, so every experiment starts from the same ground.

questions.prompt: A lender keeps 8,000 loan applications in one table with columns income, years_employed, and defaulted (yes or no). The team follows these steps. Step 1: confirm income is a number and defaulted is yes or no. Step 2: count missing income values, which comes to 64 rows. Step 3: fill those missing incomes with the median income of the training rows only, and write the rule down. Step 4: split by application month, with the oldest 70 percent for training, the next 15 percent for validation, and the newest 15 percent for test. Step 5 is missing. Which action completes the process so every later experiment starts from the same ground?
choices: Overwrite the raw application file with the filled-in values to save storage space
Recompute the median income over all 8,000 rows so the fill value matches the full table
Shuffle the rows randomly each time an experiment runs so the model sees a fresh order
Save a dated, versioned snapshot of the split and the fill rule so later runs reuse them exactly
questions.why: A dated, versioned snapshot with a fixed split and a recorded cleaning rule lets experiments be compared honestly and rerun to the same result.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket table has columns ticket_text, product_area, and hours_to_resolve. The team wants a model that predicts how many hours a new ticket will take to close. Which column is the label?
choices: product_area
ticket_text
The row number
hours_to_resolve
questions.why: The label is the answer the model learns to predict, here hours_to_resolve, while the other columns are inputs the model may use as features.

questions.prompt: A team has 12,000 photos of packaged goods stored in one folder. Each label is written only in the file name, and there is no manifest table. What is the main risk?
choices: The images will take too much disk space to train on
The model will be unable to read the image files
Labels and splits cannot be reproduced reliably, so two experiments may not be compared honestly
The validation set will automatically grow larger than the training set
questions.why: A manifest lists each file path, its label, and its split, so without it the same fixed setup is hard to recreate and comparisons become unreliable.

questions.prompt: A team has 3,000 customer reviews stored one review per file, each labeled positive or negative. Before training, which exploration step best fits the goal?
choices: Average the character length of all reviews and delete any review longer than the mean
Merge all reviews into one long document so the model sees the whole set at once
Start training immediately and check the label counts only if accuracy looks wrong
Count how many reviews carry each label and read a sample of reviews
questions.why: Exploring means looking before modeling, and label counts plus a sample of documents reveal imbalance and data problems early.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would organize a tabular dataset, a text dataset, and an image dataset so that an experiment can be repeated next month and the model can be served later. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: For tabular data I would keep one row per example with a stable ID, a documented schema, and a label column, then save a dated snapshot. For text I would keep the raw documents unchanged, store any cleaned version separately, and record the language. For images I would keep the files in one location and use a manifest table listing each path, label, and split. In all three cases I would fix the train, validation, and test split once and record it, and I would compute any scaling or cleaning rules only on the training portion, then reuse those same rules at serving time. The tradeoff is storage and upkeep: each snapshot takes space, and a manifest or split file can drift out of date if someone adds images without updating it. Splitting by time or by entity can also reduce how well the test numbers look, but it gives a more honest picture of production.
rubricPoints: Each data type has a clear structure: rows and a schema for tables, documents with recorded language for text, and files plus a manifest for images.
Splits are fixed and recorded so experiments can be compared and repeated.
Preprocessing rules are fit on training data only and reused at serving time to avoid leakage and skew.
Raw data is kept unchanged, with versioned snapshots, so earlier results can be reproduced.
A real tradeoff is named, such as storage cost, manifest drift, or lower but more honest scores.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly organizing concepts and recognizing which storage and preparation approach fits each data type, and no listed mission or planned engine practises ML data organization directly.

lessons.plain: Before a model can learn anything, raw data usually has to be cleaned, joined and reshaped. This step is called preprocessing. Google Cloud offers several tools for it, and they differ mainly in how much data they can handle and how complicated the steps can be. One tool answers questions over huge tables with plain SQL, one runs pipelines that process data as it arrives, one spreads heavy work across many machines, and one is a Python library that works within a single machine's memory. Choosing well means matching the size of the data, how fast it arrives, and the kind of logic you need, rather than picking the tool you already know best.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a nightly table of 50 GB of transactions that must be summarised by customer before training, and a separate stream of click events that must be counted every minute. Without knowing the tools, which of these two jobs do you think needs a different kind of tool, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. Preprocessing means turning raw data into the clean, joined, numeric form a model can use. A managed service is one that Google runs for you, so you do not patch or size its machines. A cluster is a group of machines that share one job. Batch processing handles a fixed set of data at once, such as last night's table. Streaming processing handles records as they arrive, such as clicks or sensor pings. In memory means the data must fit inside the RAM of the machines doing the work. A pandas script is a Python library for tables held in memory on one machine.

Why the choice matters: each tool trades scale against effort and flexibility. BigQuery is a serverless data warehouse where you write SQL and it spreads the query across its own infrastructure, so it suits batch aggregation and joins over very large tables. Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines as a managed service that handles both batch and streaming, and suits multi-step logic on continuous input. Apache Spark runs distributed jobs across a cluster; it fits when a team already has Spark code or needs its libraries, but someone must size and manage that cluster.
