It runs a graph of steps, each one a containerized component, in a fixed order, records every run, and can be triggered on a schedule or by an event. It gives repeatability and gates, but it adds setup and operational overhead. The rule of thumb is to follow the data and the repetition. Worked example: the data already lives in the warehouse, so the analysts run a SQL statement that trains a time-series forecasting model on it, then schedule that query weekly. Step one, the data stays put. Step two, the model is trained with SQL. Step three, a schedule reruns it. If later they need custom feature code, a validation check that blocks a worse model, and an approval step, they move that flow into a pipeline. Common mistake: building a pipeline for a one-off experiment, which adds orchestration work with no repeatability benefit. Consequence: a pipeline that skips its evaluation step can deploy a weaker model without anyone noticing, so the gate must be part of the graph.

questions.prompt: A regional bank keeps its loan repayment history in BigQuery. The risk team wants a classifier that predicts default, retrained every Monday, with two added requirements: an approval step that a risk officer signs before any new model replaces the live one, and a run history kept for auditors. Step one: the repayment table stays in BigQuery, so the data does not move. Step two: the classifier is trained with a SQL statement inside BigQuery ML, so no separate training service is needed. Step three: [missing]. Step four: the weekly run is triggered on a schedule and every run is recorded.
choices: Export the repayment table to a spreadsheet on a laptop and retrain the model there by hand each week.
Switch to Agent Platform AutoML, because its search over model designs will make the approval unnecessary.
Move the flow into Agent Platform Pipelines so the evaluation and approval gate is a graph step, and every run is recorded.
Keep the weekly SQL query and add a comment in the query text saying that approval is required.
questions.why: An approval gate that must run in a fixed order and leave an audit record is the orchestration need that Agent Platform Pipelines covers, so the missing step is to move the flow into a pipeline with the gate as a graph step.

questions.prompt: A small clinic has 25,000 labeled X-ray images sorted into folders by diagnosis and wants a strong first model with very little code and no custom architecture work. Which product fits best?
choices: Agent Platform Pipelines, because it runs containerized steps in a fixed order.
A hand-written training script on a single workstation, because it gives full control of the model internals.
Agent Platform AutoML, because it is a managed low-code service that searches model designs over a labeled dataset.
BigQuery ML, because images can be loaded as rows in a SQL table.
questions.why: AutoML is the managed low-code choice for a labeled dataset such as categorized images, giving a strong baseline with little code, while the other options either do not fit image data or are orchestrators rather than training services.

questions.prompt: A retail analyst runs a one-off experiment on a single sales table already in BigQuery to see whether a model is worth building at all. The team considers wrapping the experiment in an Agent Platform Pipeline with scheduled runs and an evaluation gate. What is the main problem with that choice?
choices: AutoML would be required for any experiment that has a scheduled trigger.
Nothing is wrong, because pipelines are always cheaper than running a query directly.
Pipelines cannot read data stored in BigQuery, so the experiment would fail.
The pipeline adds setup and orchestration work without giving any repeatability benefit for a run that happens once.
questions.why: A pipeline adds operational overhead, and its value comes from repetition and gates, so using it for a one-off experiment spends effort with no repeatability benefit.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a Pipelines graph that trains a demand model, then deploys it. The evaluation step that compares the new model with the current one was left out of the graph during a refactor. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The data in BigQuery will be deleted because the gate is missing.
The pipeline will fail at the deploy step with an error message, so the team notices right away.
The scheduled trigger stops running, so no new model is ever deployed.
A weaker model can be deployed without anyone noticing, because nothing in the graph blocks it.
questions.why: A gate only protects the system if it is part of the graph, so removing the evaluation step lets a worse model reach deployment silently, and the other options describe failures the missing step would not cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Agent Platform AutoML, BigQuery ML, and Agent Platform Pipelines for a new project, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with where the data lives and how often the model must be retrained. If the data is already in BigQuery and the model type on offer fits, BigQuery ML avoids copying data and lets SQL-skilled people train and predict. If we have labeled data, no ML engineers, and want a strong baseline quickly, AutoML is the low-code choice. If we need repeated training with custom code, checks that block a worse model, and approval steps, Pipelines orchestrates that workflow. I would not pick AutoML first here, because it gives less control over the model internals and its training search can cost more time and money than expected. The tradeoff is control versus effort: the more you automate, the less you can shape the result.
rubricPoints: Matches the choice to where the data lives and whether it must move
Distinguishes low-code AutoML for baselines from SQL-based BigQuery ML
Explains Pipelines as repeatable orchestration with gates and run records
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff of the option not chosen first

suggested.rationale: Choosing a product under data, skill, and repetition constraints is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no listed mission covers this.

lessons.plain: Choosing a deployment strategy means deciding how a trained model gets put in front of real users and data: whether predictions are computed on demand for each request or in a scheduled batch, how many copies of the model run, and how a new version replaces an old one without breaking anything. Think of a restaurant changing its menu. It can cook each dish to order or prepare a batch in advance, it can test a new recipe on a few tables before printing menus for everyone, and it keeps the old recipe ready in case customers complain. Those three choices, timing, capacity, and rollout, are what this objective is about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product team has a model that scores 40 million customer records once a night for a marketing email. Another team needs a score in under 100 milliseconds while a shopper waits at checkout. Without any further study, which kind of serving would you pick for each, and why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment strategy has three parts. The first is the prediction mode. Online prediction means the model answers one request at a time while a person or service waits, so latency (the time from request to answer) matters. Batch prediction means the model scores a large file or table in one scheduled job with no one waiting, so total throughput and cost matter. The second part is capacity. An endpoint is the managed address that receives requests and passes them to one or more replicas, which are running copies of the model. The minimum and maximum replica counts bound how far the service scales down and up. The third part is rollout. A traffic split sends fixed percentages of requests to different model versions. A canary release sends a small share to the new version first and widens it only while error rate and latency stay healthy.

Each choice trades one thing for another. Online serving keeps replicas warm to meet latency, but they cost money while idle. Batch serving is cheap per prediction, but its answers are only as fresh as the last run.

Worked example: a checkout fraud score needs p95 latency under 100 ms at about 500 requests per second. Step 1: choose online prediction on an endpoint. Step 2: set the minimum to 4 replicas so no shopper ever waits for a cold start, and the maximum to 12 for peaks. Step 3: deploy version 2 next to version 1 and send it 5 percent of traffic. Step 4: after an hour, if its p95 latency and error rate match version 1, raise the split to 50 percent, then 100. Step 5: if errors rise at any stage, move all traffic back to version 1 and keep version 2 for investigation.

Common mistake: setting the minimum replica count to zero to save money. The first request after an idle period then waits for a new replica to start, which can add seconds that a 100 ms target cannot absorb.

In a running system, a rollout that sends all traffic to an untested version turns a model bug into an outage of the checkout path within minutes.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer must flag which of 40 million policy records are due for renewal review. No customer or agent waits for the answer, and the job runs once a week. Step 1: choose batch prediction, because no one is waiting and total throughput and cost matter. Step 2: schedule one job each Sunday at 2 a.m. that scores the full policy table. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the flags are written to a table that the renewal team reads on Monday.
choices: Set the minimum replica count to zero so the weekly job costs nothing between runs, then add a canary split for the new model.
Send 5 percent of the policy records to version 2 of the model and compare its flags with version 1 before the job finishes.
Tell the renewal team that each flag reflects only the state of the record at Sunday's run, so changes made later in the week are not reflected until the next run.
Keep three replicas warm so that any agent who opens a policy gets an answer under 100 ms.
questions.why: Batch answers are only as fresh as the last scheduled run, so the missing step is to make that freshness limit known to the people who use the output.

questions.prompt: A product page calls a recommendation model while a shopper waits, and the team needs a reply in under 80 ms at the 95th percentile. Which prediction mode fits this need, and why?
choices: Batch prediction, because a nightly job gives the cheapest cost per prediction.
Batch prediction, because the model can score a large table once the shopper has left.
Online prediction with a minimum replica count of zero, because idle replicas cost money.
Online prediction, because a waiting service needs each request answered one at a time with low latency.
questions.why: Online prediction answers one request at a time while a service waits, so latency is the constraint that matters here.

questions.prompt: A team sets the minimum replica count of an online endpoint to zero to cut idle costs. Their latency target is 200 ms, and traffic is quiet overnight. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The batch job will score records with stale data.
The first request after an idle period waits for a new replica to start, which can exceed the latency target.
The traffic split will send too much traffic to the new version.
The endpoint will refuse all requests when the maximum replica count is reached.
questions.why: With zero warm replicas, a cold start adds seconds to the first request after idle time, which a 200 ms target cannot absorb.

questions.prompt: A team sends 30 percent of traffic to a new model version. Within minutes the new version's error rate climbs well above the old version's. What should the team do under a canary release?
choices: Raise the split to 60 percent so the error rate can be compared on more traffic.
Keep the 30 percent split and set the minimum replica count to zero to save money.
Move all traffic back to version 1 and keep version 2 available for investigation.
Delete version 1 so that all traffic goes to version 2 and the team stops comparing.
questions.why: A canary widens only while error rate and latency stay healthy, so rising errors mean returning all traffic to the stable version and investigating the new one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would roll out a new version of a model to a live service. Name the prediction mode you would assume, the rollout method, and one limit or tradeoff of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the mode. If someone or a service waits for each answer, it is online serving on an endpoint. If results can be produced in a scheduled job, batch is cheaper. For a live endpoint I would not replace the model in place. I would deploy the new version alongside the current one and send it a small share, say 5 percent, through a traffic split. I would compare its error rate and latency against the current version and widen the split in steps only while both stay within target. If something goes wrong, I move all traffic back to the old version, which is fast because it is still running. The tradeoff is cost and time: two versions run at once, and a small canary may miss rare failures, so the ramp has to be slow enough to build confidence.
rubricPoints: Names online versus batch prediction and the reason for each.
Describes a gradual traffic split or canary starting with a small share.
Explains that the old version stays running so rollback is quick.
Names a tradeoff such as duplicate running cost or small samples missing rare failures.

suggested.rationale: The planned deploy-shift engine would let the learner practise splitting traffic between versions and rolling back, which is the core skill in this objective.

lessons.plain: Some models can tell you why they made a decision and some cannot. A small set of rules you can read end to end is easy to audit, like a checklist a clerk follows. A huge neural network may be more accurate, but its reasoning is spread across millions of numbers that no person can read directly. Choosing a modeling technique against interpretability means deciding how much you need to explain a prediction, whether to a regulator, a customer, or your own team, and accepting whatever accuracy you may give up to get that explanation.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank must tell a customer the specific factors behind a loan rejection. Would you reach first for a deep neural network or a simple linear model, and why?
lessons.teach:
Interpretability means how easily a person can understand the reasons behind a model's predictions. An interpretable model is one whose internal logic can be read directly. Linear regression assigns each input feature a weight and predicts a weighted sum. Logistic regression applies the same idea and turns that sum into a probability for a yes or no outcome. A decision tree is a sequence of yes or no questions you can follow from the top node to a final answer. A black-box model, such as a deep neural network or an ensemble that combines many trees, can reach higher accuracy, but its parameters do not map to reasons a person can read.

Explainability tools try to close that gap after training. Feature attribution methods estimate how much each input feature pushed one prediction up or down. A global explanation describes the model overall, such as which features matter most across all data. A local explanation describes a single prediction. Attributions are estimates of influence, not the model's true reasoning, so treat them as evidence rather than proof.

Why it matters: when a regulator, auditor, or customer needs a reason for each decision, a model you cannot explain may be unusable regardless of its score.

Worked example: a lender must give reasons for each denied application. Step 1: a logistic regression learns a weight of plus 0.8 for debt-to-income ratio and minus 0.5 for years of employment. Step 2: applicant A has a high debt-to-income ratio, so the score falls, and the main reason is read directly from weight times value. Step 3: a neural network with similar accuracy only gives approximate attributions, which must be checked before anyone relies on them for a decision.

Common mistake: choosing the most accurate model first, then adding an explanation later, and finding the explanation too vague to satisfy the requirement. Set the interpretability requirement before comparing accuracy.

Consequence: if an unexplainable model is deployed into a regulated decision, the team may have to pull it from production when an audit asks for reasons.

Interpretability is a requirement you set up front, and it narrows which techniques are allowed.

questions.prompt: A car insurer uses a logistic regression to decide whether to offer a policy. It learned a weight of +0.6 for each prior claim and -0.2 for each year of driving experience. Applicant C has 4 prior claims and 6 years of driving. Step 1: prior claims contribute 4 times +0.6, which is +2.4, pushing toward decline. Step 2: years of driving contribute 6 times -0.2, which is -1.2, pushing toward approval. Step 3 is missing: state which reason the insurer should give the applicant for the decline.
choices: Report years of driving, because its weight is negative and negative signals drive denials.
Report prior claims, because its weight times value is the largest push toward denial.
Run a neural network on the applicant and report whichever feature it ranks first.
Average the two contributions, +2.4 and -1.2, and report the middle value as the reason.
questions.why: For one prediction in a logistic regression, the main reason is the feature whose weight times value pushes hardest toward the outcome, which here is prior claims at +2.4.

questions.prompt: A clinic must explain each referral decision to a regulator. Which model type can its logic be read directly from?
choices: A black-box model, which is accurate enough that reasons can be added after training.
An ensemble that combines hundreds of trees, since each individual tree is simple.
A shallow decision tree, whose path from the top node to the answer can be followed as yes or no questions.
A deep neural network, once post-training attribution tools have been run on it.
questions.why: A decision tree is interpretable because its yes or no questions can be followed directly from top to answer, while ensembles and neural networks do not map to readable reasons.

questions.prompt: A team trains a deep network and then uses feature attributions to justify each loan denial to an auditor. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The team should average attributions across all applicants to produce a single denial reason.
The attributions are unnecessary, because high accuracy alone satisfies audit requirements.
The attributions show the network's true reasoning, so the auditor can accept them as proof.
Attributions are estimates of influence, so they count as evidence rather than proof and may not meet a per-decision reason requirement.
questions.why: Attributions are estimates of how much features influenced a prediction, not the model's true reasoning, so they are evidence that may fall short when a per-decision explanation is required.

questions.prompt: A school district wants to know which factors matter most across all 20,000 student records for its attendance model, and separately why one particular student was flagged. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Local explanation for the overall factors; global explanation for the flagged student.
Both are local, because every record is a separate prediction.
Both are global, because attributions always describe the whole dataset.
Global explanation for the overall factors; local explanation for the single flagged student.
questions.why: A global explanation describes the model overall across all data, while a local explanation describes a single prediction, so each question needs the matching type.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes a gradient-boosted tree ensemble for loan approvals because it scores 3 points higher than logistic regression. In your own words, explain how you would decide between them, naming one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the loan decision must justify. If applicants or regulators need a clear reason for each denial, logistic regression is the safer choice, because each feature has a weight I can read and quote directly. The 3-point accuracy gain from the ensemble is real, but its reasons come from many trees combined, so any explanation is an approximation from attribution methods. I would check whether those approximations are stable across similar applicants before trusting them. The tradeoff is that I may accept a small accuracy loss to keep decisions explainable. If the business accepts approximate explanations and the accuracy gain matters more, the ensemble could be justified, but only with documented validation of the explanations.
rubricPoints: States that the interpretability requirement is set first and drives the choice
Explains that logistic regression weights can be read directly as reasons
Notes that ensemble explanations are approximations from attribution methods
Names the tradeoff of accuracy versus explainability and how to validate it

suggested.rationale: Explaining the accuracy-versus-interpretability tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Before a model can learn, its examples have to live somewhere the training job can reach them, in a shape that matches the kind of data. Spreadsheet-style rows with numbers and categories fit a table. Text, speech, images, and video are usually large files that fit better as objects in a file store, with a small table alongside describing each file and its label. Choosing well is mostly about matching the data's shape and size to the storage, so the training run is fast, cheap, and repeatable. A good answer names both where the raw files go and where the structured description goes.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 2 million rows of customer purchase records with numbers and categories, and also 300,000 product photos. Where would you put each set, and why might the same storage not suit both?
lessons.teach:
Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's object store: you keep files as objects inside containers called buckets, each addressed by a path, with no table structure imposed. BigQuery is a serverless data warehouse: you load structured data into tables and query it with SQL, and the service handles the compute scaling. Tabular data means rows and columns, such as numbers and category labels for each record. Unstructured data means items like text documents, audio, images, and video, where each item is a file. A manifest is a table that lists each file's location together with its label and its split (train, validation, or test).

Why it works: models read examples in bulk, and the reliable, cheap path is to store each kind of data where its access pattern is native. Column-oriented tables suit scanning and filtering many numeric fields. Files suit large binary content that a training job fetches by path. Keeping the manifest in BigQuery lets you filter, count, and split the file set with SQL, while the heavy bytes stay in Cloud Storage.

Worked example: a team has 1 million transaction rows and 200,000 product photos. Step 1: load the transactions into a BigQuery table, one row per transaction. Step 2: upload the photos to a bucket, grouped in folders by class. Step 3: write a manifest table in BigQuery with columns for file path, class label, and split. Step 4: query the manifest to count each class and confirm the splits are roughly balanced. Step 5: the training job reads the manifest for paths and labels, then fetches each image from the bucket.

Common mistake: putting raw image bytes or whole videos into table cells, or leaving the photos on a laptop and pointing the job at local paths. The training service cannot read those, so the run fails or the data is quietly skipped.

Consequence in a running system: if the same photo lands in both the training and test splits because the manifest was built carelessly, the reported accuracy looks better than real performance, and the team ships a model that disappoints. Splits must be fixed before training starts.

questions.prompt: A running-shoe retailer has 80,000 short product videos stored on a shared drive and a table with 80,000 rows giving each video's category and clip length. Their plan has four steps. Step 1: upload the videos to a Cloud Storage bucket, grouped in folders by category. Step 2: load the clip table into BigQuery, one row per video. Step 3 is missing from the plan. Step 4: the training job reads the manifest for paths and labels, then fetches each video from the bucket. Which Step 3 completes the plan correctly?
choices: Save the manifest as a text file on the retailer's laptop and let the training job read it from that local path.
Skip the manifest and let the job list the bucket folders, assigning splits alphabetically at training time.
Copy the videos into BigQuery table cells next to their category labels so the job needs only one data source.
Build a manifest table in BigQuery listing each video's bucket path, category label, and split, then query it to confirm no file path appears in more than one split before training starts.
questions.why: The manifest is the BigQuery table of paths, labels, and splits that the job reads, and checking for path overlap across splits before training prevents inflated accuracy while the video bytes stay in the bucket.

questions.prompt: A small museum digitises 3,000 scanned letters as image files and keeps a spreadsheet of each letter's date and donor. Which placement matches how the course describes storing this data on Google Cloud?
choices: Both the images and the spreadsheet kept in one folder on a staff member's laptop for the training job.
Both the images and the spreadsheet loaded into a single BigQuery table with the image bytes in one column.
Letter images as objects in a Cloud Storage bucket, and the date and donor fields as a BigQuery table.
Letter image bytes pasted into BigQuery table cells, with the donor fields kept in the bucket as text.
questions.why: Files such as images are stored as objects in a bucket, while structured rows and columns suit a BigQuery table, and the course's rule is to keep each kind of data where its access pattern is native.

questions.prompt: A sensor company has 2 million rows of machine readings in a BigQuery table. An engineer points the training job at a folder of photos on her workstation for the image part of the dataset. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The job succeeds but trains only on the tabular rows, since images are always ignored.
The training service cannot read the local paths, so the run fails or the photos are quietly skipped.
BigQuery automatically copies the workstation folder into a bucket before training begins.
The job reads the local photos without trouble because the readings already sit in BigQuery.
questions.why: The training service fetches files from Cloud Storage by path and cannot read a laptop or workstation, so pointing at local paths either fails the run or silently drops the data.

questions.prompt: A team builds a manifest from a table of 10,000 product photos, but the same photo appears in two rows under different file names, and each row gets its split assigned at random. What is the main risk when they train and evaluate the model?
choices: The split column becomes unreadable, so the training job cannot tell train rows from test rows at all.
BigQuery refuses to store rows whose split values were assigned randomly, so the manifest load fails.
Cloud Storage automatically deduplicates the photos, so the risk disappears once the files are uploaded.
The same photo can land in both training and test splits, so reported accuracy looks better than real performance.
questions.why: Duplicate files assigned to different splits leak test examples into training, which inflates the measured accuracy and leads to a model that disappoints in use.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should put all our training data, including the images, into BigQuery so everything is in one place. Explain to them in your own words why that is a poor fit, and name one limit or tradeoff of the split you would recommend instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: BigQuery is built to hold structured rows and columns and run SQL over them. Images, audio, and video are large binary files. Storing their bytes in table cells makes the table big and costly to scan, and the training job would have to pull and decode bytes through a query rather than reading files directly. A better split keeps the raw files in Cloud Storage, which handles large objects well and lets a job fetch each file by its path, and keeps a manifest table in BigQuery with the file path, label, and split for each item. The tradeoff is that there are now two places to keep in sync. If someone moves or deletes a file without updating the manifest, the training job fails or silently skips data. So the manifest needs a clear owner and a check that every listed path exists before training starts.
rubricPoints: Explains that BigQuery suits structured rows and columns queried with SQL, not large binary files
Explains that Cloud Storage holds large unstructured files that are fetched by path
Describes a manifest table that links each file to its label and split
Names the sync risk between the manifest and the files, and a check that prevents it

suggested.rationale: Choosing storage for each data type under a cost or scale constraint is best practised as a scenario to reason through, which no current mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: This lesson is about where and how you run the code or service that learns patterns from your data. Training is the step where a model is built from example data. Google Cloud offers several routes: you can write your own training code and let a managed service run it on rented machines, have a service search for a good model with little code, run a packaged pipeline built for tabular data, or run an open-source toolkit on a Kubernetes cluster you manage. Each route trades control against effort. The skill is matching the route to the team's skills and the problem.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has a working training script on a laptop and wants it to run on a larger machine with a GPU, without managing any servers themselves. Which Google Cloud option would you guess fits best, and why?
lessons.teach:
Definitions first. A training job is one run of code that reads data, adjusts a model, and saves the result. Custom training in Agent Platform, the Google Cloud ML service named in this objective, means you supply your own training code, and the service provisions the machines, runs the job, saves output to a storage location, and shuts the machines down when the script exits. You choose the machine type and optionally accelerators: GPUs, chips good at many parallel calculations, or TPUs, Google's accelerators for neural network math. A pre-built container is a ready-made runtime with a common framework already installed. A custom container is an image you build yourself with your own dependencies.

AutoML is a service where you supply labeled examples and the service tries many model types and settings for you, so you write little or no model code. Tabular Workflows is a packaged pipeline for tabular data, meaning rows and columns, that chains steps such as feature handling, model search, training and evaluation, and it runs on Agent Platform Pipelines. Kubeflow is an open-source toolkit for machine learning on Kubernetes, the system that schedules containers across a cluster. Kubeflow on GKE means you run it on Google Kubernetes Engine, where you still manage the cluster.

Worked example: a team has a scikit-learn model that predicts equipment failure from a 2-million-row CSV file. Step one: the code already works locally, so they package it and choose custom training with a pre-built scikit-learn container on one CPU machine. Step two: they submit the job through the Python SDK, the gcloud command line, or the console. Step three: the service starts the machine, runs the script, writes the model file to Cloud Storage, and stops the machine. The team pays only for the minutes the job ran.

Common mistake: choosing AutoML because it is easier, then discovering it cannot express the custom loss function the business needs. The consequence in a running system is that a model retrained on a schedule must be reproducible without manual steps, so the chosen route has to be one the team can repeat unattended. Picking the route is a decision about control, effort and repeatability, made before any code runs.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a scikit-learn model that scores 800,000 shipment rows stored in a CSV file. It needs one extra package, a geospatial library, that the pre-built scikit-learn container does not include. The team's path so far: Step one, they confirm the model code runs locally with that library installed. Step two, they build a custom container image that includes the library and store it where the training service can pull it. Step three is missing. Which action completes the path so the service runs their code?
choices: Submit a custom training job through the SDK, gcloud or the console that points to the custom container image
Install the Kubeflow toolkit on a GKE cluster and run the script as a notebook
Choose the pre-built scikit-learn container again and install the package at runtime
Convert the job to AutoML Tabular so the library is no longer needed
questions.why: A custom container is the image the service runs, so the job must be submitted with a reference to that image, and the service then starts it on the chosen machine.

questions.prompt: Which option is a packaged pipeline for tabular data that chains feature handling, model search, training and evaluation, and runs on Agent Platform Pipelines?
choices: A custom container
Kubeflow on GKE
AutoML image classification
Tabular Workflows
questions.why: Tabular Workflows is the packaged tabular pipeline described in the text, while the other options are either a different AutoML product for images, a toolkit that runs on a cluster you manage, or an image you build yourself.

questions.prompt: A research group has a PyTorch neural network that trains on 300 GB of labeled images and must finish within one day. Which setup fits that constraint best?
choices: Running the script on a laptop and copying the model file by hand
Custom training with a GPU accelerator on a suitable machine type, saving output to Cloud Storage
AutoML Tabular Workflows on a CPU-only machine
A pre-built container on a single CPU machine with no accelerator
questions.why: Neural network math benefits from accelerators such as GPUs, and custom training lets the team choose the accelerator and machine type, then has the service save output and shut the machines down when the script exits.

questions.prompt: A team runs Kubeflow on GKE for their model training. A month later they notice the cluster's machines are still running when no jobs are active. What best explains this?
choices: The custom container was never removed from the image registry
AutoML reserves the machines for the next model search
Tabular Workflows keeps machines running between pipeline steps
Kubeflow on GKE means the team manages the cluster itself, so its machines stay up unless they are scaled down
questions.why: Running Kubeflow on GKE means the team still manages the cluster, unlike custom training where the service shuts machines down when the script exits, so idle capacity must be handled by the team.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between custom training, AutoML, Tabular Workflows and Kubeflow on GKE for a new tabular model, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking who writes the model code and how much control we need. If we already have training code in scikit-learn or PyTorch and need a GPU or a specific machine size, I would use custom training, since the managed service runs our code and bills only while the job runs. If we have labeled tabular data and no model code, AutoML or Tabular Workflows fits better, because the service searches model types and settings for us. I would avoid Kubeflow on GKE unless the team already runs Kubernetes and needs portability, because then we would own the cluster, its upgrades and its scaling. The tradeoff with AutoML is limited control: if we need a custom loss function or an unusual architecture, the search space will not contain it, so I would move to custom training.
rubricPoints: Chooses the route based on whether the team has its own training code and how much control it needs
Explains that custom training runs the team's code on managed machines and bills only while the job runs
Names the operational burden of Kubeflow on GKE, since the team manages the cluster
States a concrete limit of AutoML, such as no custom loss function or architecture

suggested.rationale: This objective is product selection and console or SDK facts with no listed mission or planned engine that exercises it directly.

lessons.plain: When a machine learning training job fails, it stops before producing a usable model, or it finishes with a broken one. Troubleshooting means reading the clues the job leaves behind, such as error messages, logs, and progress charts, and deciding which of a few common families of problem caused it. Those families are resources (the job ran out of memory or quota), data (the input was missing or had an unexpected shape), and numbers (the training math became unstable). Fixing the right family quickly is the skill here. Throwing a bigger machine at every failure wastes money and hides the real cause.
lessons.guessPrompt: A training job that ran fine on a small sample now fails partway through the full dataset with an error saying the device ran out of memory. Before reading anything else, what would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A training failure is a training job that stops with an error, or keeps running but never learns anything useful. Training repeatedly feeds example data through a model and adjusts the model's internal numbers, called weights, so its predictions improve. An accelerator is a chip built for the large matrix arithmetic training needs, such as a GPU (graphics processor) or a TPU (tensor processing unit). Accelerator memory is limited. Each training step holds a batch, the group of examples processed together, plus the model and its intermediate results.

Most failures fall into three families. Resource failures include running out of accelerator memory, hitting a project quota (a cap on how much you may use), or a spot machine being reclaimed by the cloud provider, which is called preemption. Data failures include a file path that does not exist, a column whose type changed, or input that does not match what the code expects. Numerical failures appear as a loss value that becomes NaN (not a number). The loss is a single number measuring how wrong predictions are, and NaN means the math overflowed, often because the learning rate (the size of each adjustment) is too high or the input holds bad values.

The error text and timing usually point to the family. An out-of-memory error that appears only after a larger batch size is a resource problem. A failure on the very first step points to data or configuration. A loss that jumps to NaN points to numerics.

Worked example: a job with batch size 512 fails at step 40 with an out-of-memory error on one GPU. Step one: the message is a memory error, so the family is resources. Step two: check what changed, and find the batch size was raised from 128. Step three: choose the smallest fix, halving the batch to 256, or using gradient accumulation, which combines the adjustment signals from several small batches before each update. Step four: rerun and watch memory use.

Common mistake: moving to a larger, more expensive accelerator before reading the log. This costs more and can hide a data problem that will fail later.

Consequence: a preempted spot job without saved checkpoints, which are snapshots of model state, restarts from zero, so one failure can double the cost of the run.

questions.prompt: A demand-forecasting team at a regional grocery chain trains a model on one TPU. The job runs for 900 steps with a steadily falling loss, then the loss prints as NaN at step 901. The team's notes say the learning rate was raised from 0.001 to 0.1 two days ago. Step one: the loss became NaN, so the failure belongs to the numerical family. Step two: the learning rate was raised by a factor of 100, which is the likely cause. Step three is missing. Which action completes the trace?
choices: Buy a larger TPU so the overflow has more room to resolve
Add more examples to each batch so the gradient averages out
Switch the job to preemptible machines to save money while it reruns
Return the learning rate to a smaller value, then rerun and watch whether the loss stays finite
questions.why: A NaN loss from an overflow is fixed by the smallest change that removes the cause, which here is lowering the too-high learning rate and confirming the loss stays finite on rerun.

questions.prompt: A training job has been running for six hours. It has not stopped with an error, but its loss has not improved at all. Under the course's definition, how should this be classified?
choices: A numerical failure, because the loss must have become NaN
A resource failure, because the accelerator must be saturated
Not a training failure, because the job has not stopped with an error
A training failure, because the job keeps running without learning anything useful
questions.why: The definition of a training failure includes a job that keeps running but never learns anything useful, even when no error is raised.

questions.prompt: A training job runs on a spot machine with no saved checkpoints. Partway through, the cloud provider reclaims the machine. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The run fails with a NaN loss because preemption corrupts the weights
The run resumes at the exact step where it stopped, because weights stay in accelerator memory
The run restarts from zero, so the completed work is lost and the cost of that work is paid again
The run moves to a larger accelerator automatically and finishes at no extra cost
questions.why: Without checkpoints, which are snapshots of model state, a preempted job has nothing saved to resume from, so it restarts and repeats the cost.

questions.prompt: A team's job fails on its very first step with a message that a file path does not exist. A colleague suggests buying a bigger GPU because the job is probably short on memory. What is the better response?
choices: Lower the learning rate, since a missing file usually means the loss is about to become NaN
Raise the batch size so more examples are processed in each step
Check the file path and the job configuration first, since a first-step failure points to data or configuration
Buy a larger accelerator, since memory is the most common cause of any early failure
questions.why: A failure on the very first step together with a missing-path message points to a data or configuration problem, so the path and config should be checked before changing hardware.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the fix for every failed training job is a bigger GPU. Explain to them how you would sort a failure into its likely cause, and name one limit of your method.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the error message and when it happened, not from the hardware. I sort failures into three families: resource, data, and numerical. Resource failures such as out-of-memory errors or quota errors are usually fixed by reducing the batch size, using gradient accumulation, or requesting more quota; a bigger accelerator is one option, not the default. Data failures often appear at the first step or with a schema or missing-file message, so I check paths, column types, and whether training data matches what the code expects. Numerical failures show up as a NaN loss, so I lower the learning rate and check inputs for missing or extreme values. The limit of this method is that some failures mix families. For example, bad data can produce huge values that later cause memory growth. So I confirm each guess with one controlled rerun before changing several things at once.
rubricPoints: Sort the failure into resource, data, or numerical families using the error text and timing
Name a targeted fix for each family instead of defaulting to a bigger machine
Explain that a failure can mix families, so each guess needs a controlled check
Mention that checkpoints limit the cost of preemption or restarts

suggested.rationale: Troubleshooting depends on reasoning from symptoms to cause in an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML training.

lessons.plain: A model has two kinds of settings. Some are learned from data during training, such as the weights inside a neural network. Others are chosen by the engineer before training starts, such as how big each adjustment step is or how many examples the model looks at per step. Those chosen settings are called hyperparameters. Tuning them means trying several combinations, training a model for each one, and keeping the combination that does best on data the model was not trained on. It works like adjusting the oven temperature and baking time before you bake, then tasting each batch to find the best recipe.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a model's learning rate is set too high, what do you expect to happen to its error during training, and how would you find a better value without already knowing the answer?
lessons.teach:
A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training starts. It controls how training runs but is not learned from the data. Common examples are the learning rate, which sets how large each adjustment step is; the batch size, which sets how many examples are used per step; the number of layers or trees; and the number of passes over the training data, called epochs. A parameter, by contrast, is a value the training process learns, such as the weights in a network.

Hyperparameter tuning is the search for the combination of these choices that gives the best result on a validation set. The validation set is data held back from training and used only to compare trials. Each trial trains a model with one combination and records a score, such as validation loss. Grid search tries every combination from a fixed list. Random search samples combinations at random and often finds good settings with fewer trials. Bayesian-style optimization uses earlier results to pick promising next trials. Early stopping ends a trial once its validation score stops improving, which saves compute.

Worked example. Suppose you tune only the learning rate and try 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001. Step 1: train at 0.1; validation loss is 0.82 and rises during training, so the step is too large. Step 2: train at 0.01; validation loss falls to 0.31. Step 3: train at 0.001; loss falls to 0.35 but more slowly, needing more epochs. Step 4: choose 0.01 because it has the lowest validation loss, then score the untouched test set once to report the result.

Common mistake: choosing settings by looking at the test set, which makes the reported score optimistic. Keep the test set out of every tuning decision.

In a running system, a model tuned this way can look excellent offline and then disappoint in production. Every extra trial costs compute time and money, so budgets and early stopping matter as much as the final score.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud team trains a gradient-boosted tree model, which is an ensemble of decision trees built one after another, and tunes the maximum tree depth, meaning how many levels each tree may grow. They hold back 20 percent of transactions as a validation set, used only to compare trials, and keep a separate test set. Step 1: depth 3 gives a validation score of 0.74, where higher is better. Step 2: depth 6 gives 0.81. Step 3: depth 10 gives 0.79, and its training score climbs while validation falls, a sign it is memorising examples rather than generalising. Step 4: depth 6 has the highest validation score, so it is selected. Step 5 is missing. Which step completes the process correctly?
choices: Pick the depth whose test score is highest, since the test set is the final judge
Retrain depth 10 on the test set so its score can be compared with depth 6
Score the untouched test set once using depth 6 and report that result
Average the validation and test scores of all three depths and report the mean
questions.why: After the chosen setting is fixed on the validation set, the test set is scored once with that setting so the reported result is not inflated by tuning.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a hyperparameter rather than a learned parameter?
choices: The weights a neural network learns from the training data
The validation loss recorded at the end of a trial
The test score reported once at the very end
The batch size, which is set before training starts
questions.why: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training begins, such as batch size, while weights are values the training process learns.

questions.prompt: A team picks a learning rate by checking which of ten trials gives the best test score, then reports that same test score as the final result. What is the main problem with the reported number?
choices: Learning rate cannot be tuned on any dataset
The test set was used to make tuning decisions, so the reported score is optimistic
The test set should have been larger than the training set
Ten trials is too few to produce any valid learning rate
questions.why: Using the test set to choose settings lets the selection fit to it, so the score reported from it overstates how the model will do on new data.

questions.prompt: A recommendation model trial has a validation loss that has not improved for eight epochs in a row, and the team has a limited compute budget. Which action fits best?
choices: Switch the test set to the validation set for this trial
Stop the trial early and move the budget to other trials
Keep the trial running until the epoch limit to be safe
Restart the trial with a larger batch size without recording its score
questions.why: Early stopping ends a trial once its validation score stops improving, which saves compute that can then go to other combinations.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only trained one model by hand what hyperparameter tuning is, why the validation set rather than the test set should drive the choice, and one limit or cost of tuning.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hyperparameter tuning means choosing the settings we fix before training, like learning rate or batch size, by training several versions and comparing them. Parameters are different because training learns them from data. For each combination we train a model and record its validation loss, which is a score on data held back from training. We pick the combination with the best validation score. The test set must stay untouched during this, because if we use it to choose settings, the final score we report becomes too optimistic and tells us little about production. One limit is cost: every trial uses compute, and a large search over many settings can be slow and expensive, so we often use random search or early stopping to limit the number of trials. Tuning also cannot fix a model type or dataset that is wrong for the problem.
rubricPoints: Defines a hyperparameter as a setting chosen before training, distinct from learned parameters
Explains that candidates are compared on a validation set, not the test set
Notes that the test set is used once to report the final result to avoid optimistic bias
Names a real limit or cost, such as compute spend per trial or diminishing returns from search

suggested.rationale: Choosing which search strategy and stopping rule fits a cost or time constraint is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which no listed mission or planned engine covers.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large AI model that someone has already trained on huge amounts of general material, such as text. Fine-tuning means taking one of those models and training it further on your own examples so it behaves the way your task needs. Before you do that, ask whether clearer instructions or reference documents would already solve the problem, because tuning costs time, data and money. This lesson is about recognising when tuning is the right step and when it is not.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team's chatbot answers correctly but keeps writing replies in a different layout from the company template, even though the instructions describe the layout exactly. Before reading on, what would you try first, and what would make you consider changing the model itself?
lessons.teach: A foundation model is a large model pretrained on broad data and offered as a starting point. Model Garden is the catalogue in Agent Platform, Google Cloud's service for building and running AI workloads, where you find such models. Fine-tuning is further training of a foundation model on your own labelled input and output examples. It changes the model's internal weights so its default behaviour shifts toward your examples. It works because the model already understands language, so it needs far fewer examples than training from scratch. Three cheaper options come first. Prompting means writing clearer instructions or examples in the request and changes nothing in the model. Retrieval means fetching relevant documents at request time and adding them to the prompt, which suits facts that change. Tuning is warranted when the problem is a consistent behaviour that prompting cannot hold, such as a fixed output format, a house style, or specialised terminology repeated across many calls. Worked example: a team needs ticket summaries in a fixed layout. Prompting gets the layout right 85 percent of the time. The team collects 2,000 reviewed summary pairs, sets 200 aside as a held-out test set the model never trains on, tunes a copy of the model on the rest, then measures layout accuracy on the 200. It reaches 99 percent against the prompting baseline, so tuning is justified. Common mistake: tuning to teach the model new facts. Examples do not reliably install facts, and the knowledge goes stale, so retrieval is the right tool there. Consequence: a tuned model is a new artifact you must version, evaluate and redeploy, and re-check whenever the base model is updated or retired. Tuning is a tool for behaviour, not for knowledge.

questions.prompt: A seed catalogue company wants its shopping assistant to write product codes in the fixed pattern SD, a dash, four digits, a dash, and one capital letter, always in the same friendly tone. Nobody has yet measured how often prompting alone gets this right. The team has 1,200 reviewed assistant replies. Step one: confirm the problem is a consistent behaviour, not changing facts. It is, because the code pattern never changes. Step two is missing. Step three: tune a copy of the foundation model on 1,000 of the replies and keep 200 unseen. Step four: the tuned copy gets 98 percent of the codes right on the 200 unseen replies, so the team concludes tuning is justified.
choices: Add the current product catalogue to every prompt so the model knows which codes exist.
Train a model from scratch on the 1,200 replies, since fine-tuning does not need a foundation model.
Measure how often prompting alone gets the pattern right on a held-out set the model never trains on, so the tuning gain has a number to beat.
Skip any baseline and tune immediately, because format problems always justify tuning.
questions.why: Without a measured prompting baseline on unseen examples, the 98 percent result cannot be shown to be an improvement, so measuring that baseline is the missing step.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines fine-tuning as used in this course?
choices: Storing a model's previous answers in a cache so repeated questions return faster.
Fetching the latest policy documents at request time and adding them to the prompt.
Writing a longer, more detailed instruction in each request so the model follows a house style.
Further training of a foundation model on your own labelled input and output examples, which changes its internal weights.
questions.why: Fine-tuning is defined in the text as further training on your labelled examples that changes the model's internal weights, while the other options describe prompting, retrieval, or caching.

questions.prompt: A bank wants its assistant to answer questions about this year's tax rules. The rules were updated last month and will change again next year. Which approach fits best, and why?
choices: Tune the model on the rule documents once and never update it, since fine-tuning permanently stores facts.
Tune the model on last year's answers so it memorises the rules, then redeploy each year.
Use retrieval, fetching the current rule documents at request time and adding them to the prompt, because facts that change are better served this way than by tuning.
Use a larger model with no other changes, because bigger models always know newer facts.
questions.why: Changing facts go stale when baked into weights, so retrieval supplies current text at request time, which is the tool the course assigns to knowledge rather than tuning.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's assistant makes about 10,000 calls a day. Its replies use inconsistent terms for the same thing, such as 'pallet', 'skid' and 'platform', and prompting has not stopped this. The firm has 3,000 reviewed replies. What is the most suitable next step?
choices: Increase the number of prompt examples until the terms stop varying, without measuring anything.
Tune a copy of the foundation model on the reviewed replies, holding some back to measure terminology consistency against the prompting baseline.
Stop using the assistant, since terminology inconsistency cannot be fixed with any method.
Replace the assistant with a model trained from scratch on general web text.
questions.why: Repeated specialised terminology across many calls is a consistent behaviour that prompting cannot hold, so tuning is warranted, provided it is evaluated on held-out examples against the prompting baseline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to machine learning when your team should fine-tune a foundation model instead of improving the prompt or adding retrieval, and name one limit or tradeoff of tuning.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the cheapest fix. If the model gets the content right but the format or tone is inconsistent, and the same pattern repeats across thousands of calls, tuning is a reasonable step, because it builds the behaviour into the model and can shorten prompts. Before that, I would check whether a clearer prompt with a couple of examples fixes it. If the problem is missing or changing facts, I would use retrieval instead, since examples do not reliably teach facts. The main tradeoff is data and upkeep. Tuning needs a good set of labelled examples and a held-out test set to prove it helped. A tuned model is also a separate artifact that we must version, evaluate and redo when the base model changes.
rubricPoints: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights using labelled examples, unlike prompting or retrieval.
Tune when the problem is consistent behaviour such as format or style that prompting cannot hold.
Try prompting first, and use retrieval for facts that change.
Tuning needs quality labelled data and a held-out set to measure whether it helped.
A tuned model adds versioning, evaluation and maintenance work when the base model changes.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between prompting, retrieval and tuning is a judgement the learner must put into their own words, and no listed mission practises it.

lessons.plain: Your model needs computing power to learn from data, and the chip doing that math matters. A CPU (central processing unit) is the general-purpose processor in any computer: a modest number of powerful cores, very flexible, good at varied work done step by step. A GPU (graphics processing unit) is an accelerator with thousands of smaller cores that run the same simple arithmetic on many numbers at once. A TPU (tensor processing unit) is a chip Google designed for the large matrix operations behind deep learning. Choosing among them is a trade between speed, cost, and how easily your code runs on each. The right answer depends on what you train and how much you can spend.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you must train two models: a gradient-boosted decision tree on a spreadsheet of 2 million customer rows, and an image classifier using a deep neural network on 3 million photos. Which one would you expect to benefit most from a GPU, and why?
lessons.teach:
A CPU is the general-purpose processor in any server. It has a modest number of powerful cores that handle varied work efficiently. A GPU is an accelerator, meaning an extra chip added to do one kind of work faster, with thousands of smaller cores that run the same simple arithmetic on many numbers at once. A TPU, sold as Cloud TPU, is an accelerator Google built around matrix multiplication, the core operation of neural networks. A matrix is a grid of numbers, and a tensor is the general name for such grids in many dimensions.

Why it works: neural network training is mostly repeated multiplication of large grids of numbers. Work that splits into thousands of identical, independent pieces runs well in parallel, so GPUs and TPUs finish far sooner than a CPU. Work that branches constantly, runs in sequence, or waits on input gains little from them.

Worked example: training an image classifier. Step 1: a batch (a group of examples processed together) of 256 photos is loaded from storage. Step 2: the network multiplies that batch through many layers, which means thousands of identical matrix operations. Step 3: a GPU spreads those operations across its cores, finishing each step in a fraction of the CPU time. Step 4: for a gradient-boosted tree on a 50,000-row table, the work is mostly comparing values and branching, so a CPU is usually the cheaper and sufficient choice.

Common mistake: buying an accelerator for a job limited by data loading or preprocessing. The expensive chip then sits idle waiting for input while the hourly bill keeps running. TPUs add a constraint: they favor fixed tensor shapes and supported frameworks, and frequent shape changes force recompilation that slows training.

Consequence: in a running training pipeline, check accelerator utilization next to cost per hour. If utilization is low, the bottleneck is elsewhere, and a bigger chip only wastes money. Match the hardware to the shape of the math, and verify utilization before scaling up.

questions.prompt: A logistics company trains a neural network that predicts late deliveries from truck sensor readings. Step 1: the team runs training on a machine with four GPUs, which are accelerators (extra chips that speed up one kind of work). Step 2: the team's monitoring page shows GPU utilization (the share of time the chip is busy doing math) near 8 percent, while the hourly bill stays high. Step 3: a profile of the run shows the input pipeline, the code that reads and decompresses files on the CPU, spends most of each step on that work, so the GPUs sit waiting for data. Step 4 is missing: the team must decide what to change next. Which action fits the idea that the bottleneck should be found before the hardware is changed?
choices: Switch the job to a TPU, since TPUs always finish neural network training faster than GPUs.
Move the job to a machine with eight GPUs so the same batches finish sooner.
Fix the CPU-side input pipeline, then recheck GPU utilization before changing the hardware.
Shrink the batch size (the number of examples processed together) to 16 so the GPUs run more often.
questions.why: Low utilization with a CPU-side data bottleneck means the expensive chip is idle, so fixing the input work and rechecking utilization is the step that matches the idea, while a bigger or different chip would only add cost.

questions.prompt: A bank trains a neural network that reads scanned loan forms. Every training batch is a set of 512 by 512 pixel images, and the same layer math repeats across all of them. Which hardware choice best fits this workload?
choices: A single CPU core with the highest clock speed, because one fast core handles repeated math best.
A CPU with the most memory, because large batches only need more memory and no parallel work.
No accelerator at all, because repeated math always runs faster on storage devices.
A GPU or a TPU, because the same arithmetic repeats across many numbers at once.
questions.why: Repeated, independent matrix math splits into many identical pieces, which is the shape of work that GPUs and TPUs handle much faster than a CPU.

questions.prompt: A retail team trains a model on text reviews. Their input sentences vary in length, so each batch has a different tensor shape (the size of the grid of numbers). They move training onto a TPU and find each new shape slows the run. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The TPU does not support any kind of neural network training.
The TPU is too powerful, so it wastes time on small batches.
The reviews are stored as images, which TPUs cannot read at all.
Changing shapes forces the TPU to recompile (rebuild its compiled program), which slows training.
questions.why: TPUs favor fixed tensor shapes, and frequent shape changes trigger recompilation that slows training, which is the failure this scenario describes.

questions.prompt: A nightly job at a utilities company runs a long chain of steps. Each step waits for the previous result, and most steps branch on conditions rather than repeating the same math across many numbers. Which hardware is the usual cheapest and sufficient choice?
choices: A GPU with thousands of cores, because more cores always finish sequential work sooner.
A CPU plus an accelerator added to every step, to be safe.
A TPU, because any chain of steps runs fastest on matrix hardware.
A CPU, because work that runs in sequence and branches constantly gains little from accelerators.
questions.why: Sequential, branching work does not split into thousands of independent identical pieces, so a CPU is usually enough and an accelerator adds cost without much speedup.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between CPU, GPU and TPU for a training job, naming one limit or tradeoff of the accelerator you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the shape of the work. If the model is tree-based or linear on tabular data, or the job is dominated by parsing and joining data, a CPU is usually enough and cheapest per hour, and it avoids accelerator setup. If the model is a deep neural network with large matrix operations, a GPU is the flexible choice: it works with most deep learning frameworks and many custom operations. A TPU is worth considering for very large dense or transformer model training where the framework is supported and batches are large with stable shapes. The limit I would name for a TPU is that it rewards fixed shapes and a supported framework, and it can be slowed by recompilation or by an input pipeline that cannot feed it fast enough. Before scaling up, I would check utilization and cost per hour so we do not pay for an idle chip.
rubricPoints: CPU suits branching, sequential, or tabular work and is usually cheapest per hour.
GPU suits parallel, matrix-heavy deep learning with broad framework support.
TPU suits large neural network training with supported frameworks and stable tensor shapes.
Accelerators sit idle if data loading is the bottleneck, so check utilization against cost.

suggested.rationale: A fictional-credit cost model lets the learner compare hourly price against throughput for CPU, GPU and TPU options before committing to one.

lessons.plain: Training a machine learning model can take hours or days on one chip. Distributed training spreads that work across several chips, such as GPUs (general-purpose graphics chips widely used for AI) or TPUs (Google's custom AI chips), so the job finishes sooner or can handle a model too big for one chip. There are two main ways to split the work. One is to give every chip a full copy of the model and a different portion of the examples. The other is to cut the model itself into pieces and place each piece on a different chip. Knowing which split fits a given memory, speed, or cost limit is a core skill for this part of the exam.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one GPU needs 10 hours to train a model, what would you expect four identical GPUs to take, and what would make that estimate too optimistic?
lessons.teach:
Distributed training means running one training job across several accelerators (chips built for AI math, such as GPUs or TPUs). Data parallelism copies the whole model onto every accelerator. Each copy gets a different slice of the training batch (the group of examples used for one update), computes gradients (the numbers saying how each weight should change), and then all copies average those gradients in a communication step, so every copy applies the same update and stays identical. Model parallelism splits the model itself across accelerators, usually by placing different layers on different chips or splitting one large layer's math across chips. You need it when the weights and the extra training state do not fit in one chip's memory.

Worked example: a model copy needs 60 GB of memory and each GPU has 40 GB. Step 1: one copy does not fit, so model parallelism is required. Step 2: put the first half of the layers on GPU A and the second half on GPU B, so each holds about 30 GB. Step 3: a batch of 1,024 examples flows through A then B. Step 4: each GPU computes gradients only for the layers it holds, so no averaging across the full model is needed. Step 5: if you add a second pair of GPUs, data parallelism lets each pair handle 512 examples.

Common mistake: assuming more accelerators means proportionally faster training. Gradients must be exchanged between chips on every step, and that communication costs time. On small models or slow links, the speedup flattens while cost keeps rising. Growing the batch with the device count also often requires retuning the learning rate, the step size used during training.

In a running job, a slow interconnect shows up as accelerators sitting idle while they wait for each other, so utilization drops and the bill grows while wall-clock time barely improves. Data parallelism is the default choice when the model fits on one chip, and model parallelism is reserved for models that cannot fit.

questions.prompt: A genomics team is training a sequence model whose weights plus optimizer state total 120 GB. Each TPU chip has 32 GB of memory, so one chip cannot hold the model. Step 1: one chip is not enough, so model parallelism is required. Step 2: the team splits the layers across 4 chips, so each chip holds about 30 GB. Step 3: a batch of 2,048 sequences flows through the four chips in order. Step 4 is missing: the team wants to double training speed by adding a second group of 4 identical chips. Which strategy should they use to spread work across the two groups?
choices: Data parallelism between the two groups: each group holds a full copy of the split model, takes half the batch, and the groups average their gradients
Model parallelism again, splitting the layers across all 8 chips, because the model is still too large for one group
Swap the TPUs for chips with 80 GB each so the model fits on one chip, since mixing hardware is the fix
Nothing changes, because the second group would sit idle while the first group runs the pipeline
questions.why: Each 4-chip group already holds the whole model between them, so copies of that group can split the batch and average gradients, which is data parallelism.

questions.prompt: A computer vision model's weights and training state total 12 GB, and each GPU has 16 GB. A team has 8 GPUs and wants each epoch to finish faster. Which approach fits?
choices: Keep one GPU and enlarge the batch, since extra GPUs cannot help a model this small
Data parallelism, with one full copy on each GPU, each copy taking a different slice of the batch
Model parallelism, splitting the layers across all 8 GPUs
Model parallelism, because adding more chips always means splitting the model further
questions.why: The model fits on one GPU, so the default is data parallelism; splitting it across GPUs would add communication without solving a memory problem.

questions.prompt: A team trains a small tabular model across 16 accelerators connected by a slow network. Utilization is low, cost rose sharply, and training time barely dropped. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Gradients must be exchanged between accelerators on every step, and the slow link makes devices wait on each other
The batch is too small for any accelerator to hold
The learning rate is too high, so the gradients have become zero
The model is too large for memory, so the accelerators are constantly swapping data
questions.why: With a slow link, the time spent exchanging gradients each step dominates, so the accelerators sit idle while waiting, raising cost without speeding training.

questions.prompt: A language model needs 200 GB for its weights and training state, and each accelerator has 40 GB of memory. Which statement is correct?
choices: Data parallelism is the right first choice because it is the default regardless of memory size
Model parallelism is needed, because no single accelerator can hold the model, so layers or large layer math must be split across chips
Shrinking the batch to one example per step will let the full model fit on each accelerator
Adding more accelerators with full model copies will solve the problem, since each copy then gets its own memory budget
questions.why: Since the model exceeds one accelerator's memory, it must be split across chips with model parallelism, and shrinking the batch or copying the model does not reduce the memory each chip needs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would split the training data across accelerators instead of splitting the model across them, and name one limit of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use data parallelism when the whole model fits in one accelerator's memory but training is too slow. Each chip holds a full copy, gets a different slice of the batch, and the copies average their gradients so they all make the same update. That speeds up training roughly in proportion to the number of chips, as long as the gradient exchange stays cheap. The limit is communication. Every step, the chips must exchange gradients, so on a slow network or with a small model, adding more chips adds cost but little speed. Also, a bigger total batch often needs a retuned learning rate. If the model does not fit on one chip, I would switch to model parallelism and split layers across chips instead, accepting that data flows between chips in sequence and that a single slow layer can stall the rest.
rubricPoints: Data parallelism copies the full model to each accelerator and splits the batch across them.
Gradients are averaged so every copy applies the same update.
Model parallelism splits layers or layer math across chips and is needed when the model does not fit in memory.
Communication between chips limits how much speedup adding accelerators gives.
A larger batch across more devices often needs a retuned learning rate.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between the two parallelism strategies and stating their tradeoffs is best practised by explaining the reasoning, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML training.

lessons.plain: Deploying a model means putting a trained model where other software can ask it for answers. There are two common patterns. Online inference answers one request at a time, quickly, like a checkout page asking whether a card payment looks fraudulent. Batch inference scores a large pile of records in one job, like re-scoring every customer overnight, and writes the results somewhere to read later. Choosing where to run the model depends on which pattern you need, how much control you want over the machines, and how traffic rises and falls. Think of it as choosing between a managed restaurant kitchen, a food truck you can park anywhere, and building your own kitchen.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants a model to flag suspicious orders while the customer waits, and separately wants every past order re-scored once a night. Do you think both jobs should run the same way, and why?
lessons.teach:
Inference means using a trained model to produce a prediction. Online inference is request and response: a caller sends one input and waits for an answer, so latency (the time to answer) matters. Batch inference reads many inputs from storage, scores them in a job that runs to completion, and writes the outputs to storage. An endpoint is a network address that accepts online requests. A replica is one running copy of the model process. Concurrency is how many requests a single replica handles at the same time.

The objective names four services, and each is a different kind of runtime. The Agent Platform is the managed model-serving platform: you deploy a model to an endpoint and it runs the machines for you, and it also offers batch prediction jobs. Model Garden is a catalogue of ready-made models, including foundation models, that you can deploy or adapt instead of training from scratch. Cloud Run runs a container you build and scales its instances with incoming requests, down to zero when idle. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) runs Kubernetes, which schedules containers across a cluster of machines you configure and pay for. GKE gives the most control and the most operational work.

Throughput, the number of requests served per second, is roughly the number of replicas times the requests each replica can handle. Scaling adds replicas when load rises above a target and removes them when it falls.

Worked example: a fraud check must answer within 200 ms during checkout. It is online, so it needs an endpoint. The team has no cluster and wants managed scaling, so a managed endpoint fits. If traffic is 500 requests per second and each replica handles about 50, the backend needs about 10 replicas, and a small minimum keeps cold starts from adding delay. Rescoring 20 million accounts each night is batch, so a batch job avoids paying for idle replicas.

Common mistake: choosing GKE because it sounds most powerful, then owning cluster upgrades and node sizing for a model a managed service would serve. In a running system, scale-to-zero means the first request after an idle period waits for a cold start, which appears as a latency spike at checkout.
