The right serving target follows from the access pattern, the required latency, and how much operational work the team can carry.

questions.prompt: A stock-photo company runs a tagging model that must return labels within 150 ms each time a user uploads a photo, so the upload page waits for the answer. Peak load is 1,200 requests per second, and one replica handles about 80 requests per second. The team has no Kubernetes cluster and wants the platform to handle scaling. Step 1: the upload waits for a reply, so this is online inference and needs an endpoint. Step 2: no cluster and a wish for managed scaling point to a managed endpoint. Step 3 (missing, to be worked out): how many replicas are needed at peak. Step 4: the team sets the endpoint to scale up to that replica count when load peaks.
choices: Use 80 as the replica count and divide it by 1,200 to size the cluster
Divide 1,200 by 80 to get 15 replicas at peak, which is the number scaling must reach
Multiply 1,200 by 80 to get 96,000 replicas, since more requests means more copies of the work
Set the replica count to 1,200 so that every request gets its own copy of the model
questions.why: Throughput is roughly replicas times requests per replica, so the replicas needed at peak are the peak load divided by the per-replica rate, which is 1,200 divided by 80, or 15.

questions.prompt: A news site wants to re-label its archive of 3 million past articles with topic tags every weekend. No reader waits for these labels, and the results only need to be in storage by Monday. Which serving approach fits best?
choices: A GKE cluster sized to the constant peak load of the archive
A Cloud Run service that labels each article as a request arrives
A batch prediction job that reads the archive from storage and writes the labels back to storage
An online endpoint with a minimum of four replicas kept warm all week
questions.why: No caller waits for an answer and the work runs to completion over storage, which is the batch pattern, so a batch job avoids paying for idle replicas.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a chat helper on Cloud Run, which scales instances down to zero when idle. Users report that the first message after a quiet lunch hour hangs for several seconds, then replies are fast. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model is too large, so its accuracy drops whenever the service first starts
The batch job is writing outputs to storage during the day and slowing the endpoint
Scale-to-zero: the first request after an idle period waits for a cold start of a new instance
The concurrency setting is too low, so requests queue behind each other in one instance
questions.why: Scaling to zero means no instance is running when the idle period ends, so the first request waits while an instance starts, which shows up as a one-time latency spike.

questions.prompt: A serving backend has 6 replicas, and each replica handles about 40 requests per second at a steady load. Using the rule that throughput is roughly the number of replicas times the requests each replica handles, what is the approximate total throughput?
choices: 6.7 requests per second
240 requests per second
46 requests per second
40 requests per second
questions.why: Six replicas each handling 40 requests per second gives 6 times 40, which is 240 requests per second, so the calculation multiplies rather than divides.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a managed model endpoint, Cloud Run, and GKE for a new model, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the access pattern. If callers need an answer in a request, I need an online endpoint. If the work is a scheduled pass over many records, I use a batch job and do not keep replicas running. For online serving, I prefer the managed model endpoint when the team wants the platform to handle machines, scaling and model deployment. Cloud Run is a good fit when we already package the model in a container and want request-based scaling with little cluster work. GKE is the one I would not pick first: it gives full control over hardware such as GPUs and networking, but we would own cluster upgrades, node pools and capacity planning. The tradeoff with Cloud Run is cold starts when it scales to zero, so for a latency-sensitive path I would keep a minimum instance count. Before choosing, I would check the latency target, the expected requests per second, and how many replicas that implies.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes online inference (request-response, latency-bound) from batch inference (scheduled, throughput-bound).
Explains that a managed endpoint or batch job reduces machine operations, while GKE gives the most control and the most upkeep.
States that throughput scales with replica count times per-replica concurrency.
Names a concrete limit, such as cold-start latency on scale-to-zero or cluster ownership on GKE.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a serving target is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style scenario that weighs latency, traffic and operational effort, and no current mission covers this.

lessons.plain: When a model is trained, the result is a file of learned numbers. Serving means wrapping that file in a small program that waits for requests, loads the file once, and returns predictions. Packaging is bundling the model file together with the code that runs it. PyTorch and XGBoost each have their own file format and library, so the bundle has to match them. A prebuilt container is a ready-made runtime that the provider maintains, and you supply only the model file. A custom container is an image you build yourself when you need different code, libraries, or a different web server.
lessons.guessPrompt: A teammate trained a model in PyTorch on a laptop with one library version, then copied only the weights file to a server running a different PyTorch version and got load errors. Before reading further, what would you guess went wrong, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A model artifact is the saved file or set of files produced at training time. It holds learned parameters and sometimes the structure needed to rebuild the model. A serving container is the runtime that loads that artifact, listens for network requests, and returns predictions. A prebuilt container is a runtime image maintained by the cloud provider for a given framework and version, so you upload only the artifact. A custom container is an image you build yourself, with your own code, libraries and web server. You use it when the prebuilt runtime cannot do what you need, such as custom preprocessing or an unusual framework.

Why it works: a serving container must do three things. It loads the artifact once at startup. It answers a health check so the platform knows it is alive. It answers a predict route using the input format the model expects. The platform only sends traffic to replicas that pass the health check.

Worked example: a team saves an XGBoost model to a file. Step 1, they train the model and save it. Step 2, they confirm the XGBoost version used for training matches a prebuilt XGBoost container version. Step 3, they upload the file as the artifact and deploy it to an endpoint using that prebuilt container. Step 4, the platform starts a replica, which loads the file, passes its health check, and then serves predictions. If they also needed custom feature scaling, they would write a small HTTP server in a custom image that applies the scaling before calling the model.

Common mistake: uploading only the weights, or serving a model trained with one framework version on another version, and assuming the endpoint will work. The file format and the library version must agree.

Consequence: if a container cannot load the artifact, the replica never becomes healthy, so scaling out during a traffic surge adds no capacity. Because each new replica loads the model at startup, a large artifact also slows every scale-out event. Packaging is therefore part of scaling, not a separate step.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor, Tessaly Foods, has a PyTorch model saved as a state dict (a file holding only the learned weights, without the code that builds the network). Their model expects inputs scaled into the range 0 to 1 (min-max scaling), which the training data did not need at serving time, so they decide to package a custom container. Step 1: they build the image with PyTorch at the same version used in training and include the scaling code. Step 2: they copy the state dict file into the image as the artifact. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: they deploy the image to an endpoint, and the platform starts a replica. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: Skip the health check, since a custom image the team built itself is already trusted.
Load the artifact on every predict request so the scaling code always sees the latest file.
Send traffic to the replica immediately, then load the file in the background while requests are answered.
Write a small HTTP server that loads the artifact once at startup, answers the health check, and applies the scaling before calling the model on the predict route.
questions.why: A serving container must load the artifact once at startup, answer the health check, and answer the predict route, and the custom scaling runs inside that server before the model is called.

questions.prompt: A hospital imaging group has a PyTorch model that needs a custom decoder for its scanner file format, a library the prebuilt container does not include. Which packaging should they choose and why?
choices: Upload only the weights file, because the decoder can be added later through the endpoint settings.
Prebuilt container, because custom code can be placed inside the artifact file itself.
Prebuilt container, because the artifact alone is enough whenever the framework version matches.
Custom container, because the prebuilt runtime cannot run their extra decoding step.
questions.why: A custom container is the right choice when the prebuilt runtime cannot do a needed step such as custom preprocessing, and the decoder is exactly that kind of step.

questions.prompt: A retail company trained an XGBoost model with library version 1.7 and deploys it to a prebuilt XGBoost container for version 2.0 during a holiday sales surge. What is the most likely effect when the platform tries to scale out?
choices: The platform will add capacity normally, since the artifact file itself is valid.
The endpoint will split traffic evenly between old and new replicas with no errors.
New replicas may fail to load the artifact, so they never pass the health check and add no serving capacity.
The new replicas will serve faster because the newer library is more efficient.
questions.why: The file format and library version must agree, and a mismatch can stop a replica from loading, which keeps it unhealthy so it adds no capacity.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company's PyTorch artifact is 6 GB, and traffic doubles within minutes. Which statement about scale-out is correct?
choices: Each new replica loads the 6 GB file at startup before it can pass its health check, so scale-out is slower.
The platform sends traffic to new replicas as soon as they start, so file size only matters for storage cost.
The file is read only on the first request to each replica, so scale-out speed is unaffected.
Large artifacts make the health check unnecessary because the model is already loaded from disk.
questions.why: Each new replica loads the artifact at startup, so a large file delays the moment the replica becomes healthy and can take traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose a prebuilt serving container over a custom one for a PyTorch or XGBoost model, and name one limit or tradeoff of the custom route.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a prebuilt container whenever the model is a standard PyTorch or XGBoost model and the input needs no unusual handling. I only supply the saved artifact, and I make sure the framework version used in training matches the container version, because a mismatch is the most common reason a replica fails to load. I would move to a custom container when I need preprocessing built into the server, a library the prebuilt image lacks, or a different web server. The tradeoff is that I now own the image: I have to build it, keep its libraries patched, make sure it listens on the port and health route the platform expects, and test that it still starts quickly when replicas scale out.
rubricPoints: A prebuilt container is provider-maintained and needs only the model artifact uploaded.
A custom container is your own image, used when you need custom code, libraries, or server behaviour.
The framework and library version in training must match the serving runtime, or loading fails.
Custom containers bring ownership costs such as building, patching, health checks and startup time.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a container type from a scenario is best practised by reasoning through a situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model packaging directly.

lessons.plain: When a team trains a model, it produces a file of learned numbers. Over weeks many of these get made: a better version, a test version, one trained on last month's data. A model registry is a labelled filing cabinet for them. Each model gets a name, each saved attempt becomes a numbered version, and notes can record how it was built and how well it scored. Pointers called aliases say which version is the current one or the candidate, so people and systems can ask for the production model without memorising numbers. This matters because when something goes wrong, you need to find the exact model that was running, and go back to the one before it, quickly and without guessing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has retrained a model three times this quarter and saved each result to the same storage folder, with each new file overwriting the last. When the latest model starts giving bad predictions, what is the first thing that goes wrong when you try to recover?
lessons.teach:
A model registry is a shared catalogue where a team stores trained models so they can be found, compared and reused later. Each entry is a model with a name, and under it sit model versions: numbered snapshots such as version 1, 2 and 3. Each version points at the saved model files, which are called artifacts, and at metadata describing how it was made: the training data reference, the code version, the evaluation scores and the settings used. An alias is a human-friendly pointer, such as 'production' or 'candidate', that moves from one version to another without changing the model's name. Lineage is the recorded trail linking a version back to the data and the pipeline run that produced it.

Why this works: training is repeatable but not free, and people later need to answer which model is live and what it was trained on. A registry turns that question into a lookup instead of an investigation. Versions are treated as fixed, so version 2 always means the same files, while the alias decides which version a deployment should pick up.

Worked example. A churn model has versions 1, 2 and 3. Version 2 carries the alias 'production' and serves traffic. Version 3 scores better on evaluation, so it gets the alias 'candidate'. Step by step: register version 3 with its scores, run a small canary check, and if it passes, move 'production' to version 3. If version 3 misbehaves, move the alias back to version 2. Nothing is retrained or rebuilt.

Common mistake: uploading new files over old ones under the same version number, or deleting older versions to tidy up. Then the rollback target is gone, and nobody can say which artifact produced the number on a dashboard.

Consequence in a running system: a deployment that points at a specific version keeps serving that exact model until someone changes it. A deployment that follows an alias may pick up a newer version the next time it is updated, so how the deployment is wired decides when a change reaches users. The registry is the record that lets a team know exactly which model is live and how to return to the last good one.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's demand forecast model is registered as 'demand-forecast'. Its alias 'live' (a movable pointer that names which version serves traffic) points to version 7. An auditor asks what data trained the model users currently see. Step 1: look up the alias 'live' and find it points to version 7. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: read the training data reference recorded for that pipeline run in the metadata. What belongs in the missing step? (Lineage means the recorded trail linking a version back to the data and pipeline run that produced it.)
choices: Compare the file sizes of version 7 and version 6 to guess the data window
Ask the data team which dataset was newest in the week version 7 was made
Retrain version 7 from scratch so you can watch which data it consumes
Follow version 7's lineage link to the pipeline run that produced it
questions.why: Lineage is the recorded link from a version to the pipeline run that produced it, so following that link is what leads to the data reference, while the other options either rebuild the model or guess from indirect clues.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring team in a payments company keeps versions 12 and 13 of its model. Which description best fits an alias in the registry?
choices: A copy of version 12's files saved under a brand-new model name in the same catalogue
A permanent number stamped into the artifact files that can never be changed by anyone later on
The evaluation score recorded for each version, displayed on the team's monitoring dashboard
A movable pointer, like 'champion', that can be moved to another version
questions.why: An alias is a human-friendly pointer that can be reassigned from one version to another without changing the model's name, which is exactly what the movable pointer describes.

questions.prompt: A sentiment model team uploads new files over version 4 under the same version number, then deletes version 3 to tidy the catalogue. What is the main problem this creates?
choices: The team cannot roll back to a known-good version, and the reported score can no longer be traced to the files that produced it, because the number now refers to different files and the old version is gone
Version 4 automatically keeps its original files in a hidden cache, so nothing that matters is lost
The registry renumbers the remaining versions on its own, so dashboards and rollbacks update themselves
Only the metadata is affected, since the artifact files still match the scores recorded for each version
questions.why: Versions are meant to be fixed snapshots, so overwriting one and deleting another removes the rollback target and breaks the link between a number and its artifacts.

questions.prompt: A recommendation service's deployment follows the alias 'prod' (a movable pointer to a version) instead of a fixed version number. At 2 pm engineers move 'prod' to version 9, but the service is not redeployed. What happens?
choices: The service starts serving version 9 files that were copied into its container automatically at 2 pm
It picks up version 9 only at its next update, so the wiring sets timing.
The alias move fails until the service is redeployed with the new version number written into its configuration
Every server switches to version 9 at 2 pm, because alias moves are pushed instantly to all running deployments
questions.why: A deployment that follows an alias may only pick up the newly pointed-to version the next time it is updated, so how the deployment is wired decides when users see the change.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says: we keep one model file per name and overwrite it on each retrain, that is simpler. Explain to them what a model registry with numbered versions and aliases gives you that overwriting does not, and name one limit or tradeoff of adding this structure.
lessons.modelAnswer: Overwriting gives you one file and no history, so when a retrain turns out worse, you cannot return to the previous model without rebuilding it from old data and code, if you can rebuild it at all. A registry keeps each trained attempt as a numbered version that does not change, with its evaluation scores and the data and code that produced it. An alias such as production then points at one version, so promoting or rolling back is just moving that pointer. The tradeoff is overhead: someone has to register versions, keep metadata honest, and clean up old versions deliberately, and teams that skip this discipline end up with a registry full of unlabelled entries that nobody trusts.
rubricPoints: Versions are kept as separate, unchanged snapshots, so the previous model stays available.
Aliases point at a version, so promotion and rollback mean moving a pointer, not retraining.
Metadata and lineage record the scores, data and code behind each version.
The cost is process overhead, and the registry is only useful if metadata and cleanup are maintained.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is reasoning about versioning and rollback in your own words, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model registries.

lessons.plain: When you have a new version of a machine learning model, you usually do not switch every user to it at once. Instead you send a small slice of real traffic to the new version while the old one keeps serving the rest. A canary deployment is the cautious version of this: a small slice first, then more only if nothing breaks. An A/B test is the comparison version: two versions run side by side with traffic split between them, and you measure which one does better on what matters, such as clicks or purchases. Both approaches limit the damage from a model that looked good on saved test data but behaves badly with live inputs.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your new fraud model scored better than the old one on last month's saved test data. Would you switch all customers to it today? Why or why not, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A traffic split is the share of live requests an endpoint sends to each model version, for example 95 percent to version 1 and 5 percent to version 2. A canary deployment gives a small split to the new version, the canary, and widens it only while health checks stay normal. Those health checks are guardrail metrics, such as error rate and latency, which protect users even before anyone has judged whether the model is actually better. An A/B test has a different purpose: it splits traffic to answer a question about outcomes. The old version is the control, the new one is the treatment, and you compare a primary metric such as conversion rate. Live traffic matters because it shows how a model behaves on today's inputs, which saved test sets can miss.

Worked example. Version 1 serves 100 percent of traffic. You deploy version 2 and send it 5 percent. After one hour, version 2 has an error rate of 0.2 percent, the same as version 1, and latency inside its target. You raise it to 20 percent, then 50 percent, checking guardrails at each step. For a separate A/B test on conversion, you hold a 50/50 split for two weeks, assign each user to one group consistently, and measure 4.1 percent versus 3.8 percent conversion. You declare a winner only when the gap is larger than random variation would explain.

Common mistake: stopping early because the new version looked better after two hours, or re-randomizing users on every request so the same person sees both versions and the groups blur together.

Consequence: a 5 percent canary that is ten times slower affects one user in twenty right away. Because the old version is still running, rollback is simply moving the split back to 0 percent for version 2.

questions.prompt: A ride-pricing team has model price-v5 serving 100 percent of traffic and deploys price-v6 next to it. Their notes show the following steps: 1) send v6 4 percent of traffic; 2) after 30 minutes, confirm v6's error rate and latency match v5's; 3) raise v6 to 12 percent; 4) after 25 minutes, check the same guardrails and find v6's p95 latency at three times its target. Step 5 is missing from the notes. Which step completes the rollout process correctly?
choices: Set v6's split to 0 percent so all traffic returns to v5, which is still running and can take the load
Raise v6 to 50 percent so that the average latency across both versions falls back into range
Delete v5 so that only the version you are testing remains on the endpoint
Keep v6 at 12 percent and compare conversion rates for another week before deciding anything
questions.why: Because the old version is still running, rollback means moving the split for the new version back to 0 percent, which the team can do immediately without deleting anything.

questions.prompt: A lending company wants to know whether a new loan-approval model approves more good applicants than the current one. Which setup is an A/B test rather than a canary deployment?
choices: Replace the current model entirely and watch the health dashboard for any errors in the first day
Keep both models live at a fixed 50/50 split, assign each applicant to one group consistently, and compare approval quality as the primary metric
Send the new model 2 percent of applications and widen the share only while error rate and latency stay normal
Run the new model on a copy of last year's applications offline and compare its scores with the old model's
questions.why: An A/B test uses a fixed split between control and treatment to answer an outcome question with a primary metric, while the canary in the other choices is about guardrail health.

questions.prompt: An online bookstore sends each page view to model A or model B at random, so the same shopper can see both versions during one visit. After a week the conversion gap looks small. Why is this result hard to trust?
choices: Conversion rate cannot be measured on a bookstore, only on advertising clicks
Live traffic is never suitable for comparing two models, so any result from it is invalid
A week is too long, and conversion metrics expire after a few days
Random per-request assignment lets one person see both versions, so the groups blur together and the comparison is muddled
questions.why: Assigning users to groups inconsistently mixes the groups, which is why each user should stay in one group throughout the test.

questions.prompt: A video app sends 5 percent of traffic to a new recommendation model. After 40 minutes its error rate is 0.3 percent, while the current model's is 0.1 percent, and latency is within target. What is the right next action for the canary?
choices: Raise the split to 50 percent so the error rate averages out across both models
Declare the new model the winner because its latency is within target
Start a two-week A/B test on the same 5 percent slice to measure engagement
Hold the split at 5 percent or move it back toward 0 percent, since a guardrail metric is worse than the baseline
questions.why: A canary widens only while guardrails stay normal, so a higher error rate means the split should be held or reduced, and the old version is still there to fall back to.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a canary rollout and an A/B test of two model versions, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A canary rollout and an A/B test both send live traffic to two model versions, but they answer different questions. A canary asks whether the new version is safe to run: I send it a small share, watch error rate and latency, and widen the share only if those stay healthy. Its limit is that it tells you almost nothing about whether the model predicts better, so a canary that passes can still be a worse model. An A/B test asks which version gets better outcomes: I hold a fixed split, keep each user in one group, and compare a primary metric such as conversion. Its limit is that it needs enough traffic and time to separate a real difference from noise, and stopping early when the numbers look good can produce a false winner. In practice I run a canary first to protect users, then an A/B test once the new version is safe.
rubricPoints: A canary checks operational safety with guardrail metrics and widens traffic gradually.
An A/B test compares outcomes using a control, a treatment and a primary metric.
Each user should stay in one group so results are not blurred.
A canary alone cannot show the new model is more accurate or more useful.
A/B tests need enough traffic and time, and early stopping risks a false winner.

suggested.rationale: The planned deployment-strategies engine would let the learner set traffic splits and watch guardrails and outcome metrics, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a model is running and someone sends it a request, the raw request usually is not in the exact shape the model expects. Preprocessing is the work done to the input before the model sees it, such as scaling numbers, resizing a photo, or looking up extra facts about a customer. Postprocessing is the work done to the model's raw output afterwards, such as turning a score into a yes or no or a readable label. Both steps sit on the serving path, so they affect speed, correctness, and what users actually see.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model was trained on house prices, with square metres scaled so that the training average became 0 and the spread became 1. At serving time, someone sends a raw size in square metres and gets a nonsense price back. Where would you expect the bug to be, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
Inference preprocessing is every transformation applied to a request before the model runs. Inference postprocessing is every transformation applied to the model's raw output before the response goes back to the caller. Inference means asking a trained model for a prediction. Preprocessing examples include scaling numbers using the mean and spread learned during training, converting text into integer token IDs, resizing an image, or fetching extra features from a lookup store. Postprocessing examples include applying a threshold to a probability, mapping a class index to a human label, or rounding and formatting values.

Why this matters: a model only gives meaningful answers for the kind of input it was trained on. The transforms at serving must therefore match training exactly, and the statistics used for scaling, such as the training mean and spread, must be saved with the model rather than recomputed from live traffic.

Worked example. A churn model was trained on monthly spend scaled as (spend minus 40) divided by 20, where 40 was the training mean and 20 the training spread. A request says spend is 60. Step 1: receive 60. Step 2: subtract 40, giving 20. Step 3: divide by 20, giving 1.0. Step 4: pass 1.0 to the model, which returns a probability of 0.72. Step 5: postprocessing applies a threshold of 0.5 and returns churn risk: yes.

Common mistake: recomputing the mean and spread from serving data, or writing the transform twice, once in a notebook and once in the server. The two copies drift apart and the model silently receives values on the wrong scale. This is called training-serving skew, and it usually appears as worse accuracy in production with no error raised.

Consequence: preprocessing runs on every request, so a slow lookup there adds latency to every prediction and grows with traffic. Preprocessing and postprocessing should be packaged with the model version so one release carries the input and output rules that the weights were built with.

questions.prompt: A bike-share demand model was trained on trip distance scaled as (distance minus 4) divided by 2, where 4 was the training mean and 2 the training spread. A request gives a distance of 10 km. Step 1: receive 10. Step 2: subtract 4, giving 6. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: pass the scaled value to the model, which returns a score of 0.61. Step 5: postprocessing applies a threshold of 0.5 and returns high demand: yes. Which choice correctly fills in the missing Step 3?
choices: Recompute the mean from the 10 km in this request before subtracting
Divide by 2, giving 3.0, which is the scale the model was trained on
Multiply by 2, giving 12, because the spread is applied as a multiplier
Skip scaling because a single request is too small to need it
questions.why: Dividing by the saved training spread completes the scaling the model expects, turning 6 into 3.0.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of inference postprocessing rather than preprocessing?
choices: Resizing an image to a fixed width
Fetching extra features from a lookup store
Mapping class index 2 to the label fraud
Converting text into integer token IDs
questions.why: Turning a raw class index into a human label happens to the model's output after it runs, so it is postprocessing.

questions.prompt: A team recomputes the scaling mean and spread from the last week of live requests instead of using the values saved with the model. What is the main risk?
choices: Latency rises only during the first request after a deploy
Training-serving skew: inputs land on a different scale than training, and accuracy drops with no error raised
Accuracy stays the same because the spread is unchanged
The model refuses to run and raises an explicit error
questions.why: Live statistics differ from training statistics, so the model silently receives values on the wrong scale, which is training-serving skew.

questions.prompt: A preprocessing step makes a slow lookup to a feature store for every incoming request. What happens to the system as traffic grows?
choices: The model's weights are retrained automatically whenever the lookup responds slowly
Each prediction gets added latency, and that extra delay grows as request volume rises
Only the first prediction after startup is slowed, and later ones return to normal speed
Nothing changes, because preprocessing runs once when the server starts and is then cached
questions.why: Preprocessing runs on every request, so a slow step adds latency to every prediction and the cost grows with traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes doing all inference preprocessing in the client app so the serving backend stays thin. Explain to them what they would gain, what they would lose, and the main risk you would ask them to address before agreeing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Moving preprocessing to the client keeps the server simple and can cut server compute, since each client does its own scaling and encoding. The cost is that the transforms now live in many places, usually in several languages and app versions, and they are hard to keep identical to the training code. If one client uses an old mean or a different tokenizer, the model receives shifted inputs and predictions degrade silently. I would want the transforms versioned with the model, a shared implementation or test suite that checks client output against the training pipeline, and a way to reject requests that come from an outdated client. Postprocessing, like thresholds and label names, should usually stay on the server so that changing it does not require an app release.
rubricPoints: Preprocessing must match what the model was trained on, including saved statistics and encodings.
Moving transforms to clients adds risk of version drift and training-serving skew.
Keeping transforms on the server centralizes changes but adds per-request compute and latency.
Postprocessing such as thresholds and labels is easier to change server-side without client releases.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about where transforms live and what tradeoffs that placement creates, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: A feature is one piece of information a machine learning model uses to make a prediction, such as how many orders a customer placed this week or the average time a delivery took last month. A feature store is a shared place where a team defines these pieces of information once, computes them, keeps them up to date, and hands them out. It usually serves two needs: a large historical copy used to train models, and a fast lookup table used when a live request needs an answer in milliseconds. Its main job is making sure the model sees the same numbers during training and in production.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team trains a model on a customer's order count from last week, but at prediction time the app computes the order count a different way and gets a slightly different number. Why might this quietly hurt the model, and what would you change so both sides use one definition?
lessons.teach:
A feature is a named, computed input value tied to an entity, which is the thing being described, such as a customer or a vehicle. The entity is identified by an entity key, such as customer_id. A feature store is a managed system that holds feature definitions and values so that many models and teams can reuse them. It has two stores. The offline store keeps the full history of feature values and is used to build training datasets. The online store keeps only the latest value for each entity, indexed by its key, so a live prediction can read it in a few milliseconds.

Why it works: the main risk in production machine learning is training-serving skew, where the model learned from numbers computed one way but receives numbers computed another way. A feature store reduces this by computing a feature once, in one pipeline, and writing it to both stores. A second risk is leakage: when building training rows, you must use only the values that existed at the moment each label happened. Feature stores support point-in-time lookups for this, so a training row dated in February does not see a March value.

Worked example. A delivery-time model needs driver_avg_minutes_7d. Step 1: a nightly job computes the seven-day average for each driver and writes it to the offline store with a timestamp. Step 2: the same job pushes the latest value for each driver to the online store, keyed by driver_id. Step 3: at request time the serving code asks the online store for driver 4411 and gets one number back in a few milliseconds. Step 4: when building training data, the builder asks for the value as it was on each past trip date, not today's value.

Common mistake: teams copy the feature calculation into the serving application as a separate query or code path. The two versions drift apart over time, and accuracy drops with no error message.

Consequence: online lookups sit on the request path, so the online store's capacity must match prediction throughput. If the sync job stops, the online values go stale while predictions keep succeeding, which is why feature freshness should be monitored.

questions.prompt: A bike-sharing company tracks a feature called bike_rides_1h, which is the number of rides started at a station in the previous hour. The station is the entity, and its key is station_id. The team's pipeline works like this. Step 1: an hourly job counts rides for each station over the previous hour and writes each count to the offline store with its timestamp. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the trip-planning app reads the current value for station S-17 at request time and gets one number back quickly. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: The same job pushes the latest count for each station to the online store, keyed by station_id, so both stores come from one computation.
Once a year the full offline history is copied into the online store as a backup.
The app recomputes the hourly count from raw trip logs on every request so the value is always fresh.
The team copies the counting query into the app and runs it only when the online store has no entry for a station.
questions.why: The online store keeps only the latest value per entity key and is fed from the same computation as the offline store, which avoids the drift that comes from a second calculation path.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing company stores a feature driver_rating_30d, keyed by driver_id, in a feature store. A live dispatch service needs this value within milliseconds while choosing a driver for a new request. Which store should answer that lookup, and why?
choices: The online store, because it keeps the latest value for each driver_id and is built for quick keyed reads.
Both stores merged on every request, so the dispatcher sees the history and the latest value together.
The raw trip log in the data warehouse, because it is the original source of the rating.
The offline store, because it keeps the full history and can be scanned in a single request.
questions.why: The online store holds only the latest value per key, which is what a live request needs, while the offline store holds history meant for building training data.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain builds a training set for a demand model from sales in March. Each training row is dated 3 March, and it needs the feature promo_weeks_active. The builder fetches the value as it stands today, 14 June, for every row. What is the main problem with this?
choices: The online store will reject the lookup because the requested date is in the past.
Leakage: rows use a value that did not exist on 3 March, so offline scores overstate how well the model will do in production.
Training-serving skew is removed, because training and serving now both use today's value.
None, since the newest value is always the most accurate input for training.
questions.why: Leakage happens when training rows see information from after the label's moment, and a point-in-time lookup is what prevents it.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs an hourly job that refreshes a fraud feature for each merchant in the online store. The job has failed for two days, but the scoring service keeps returning successful responses. What is the main risk?
choices: Predictions use stale feature values without any error, so feature freshness should be monitored.
The online store deletes all values after one day, so every later lookup will fail with an error.
There is none, because the scoring service falls back to the offline store automatically during serving.
The offline store overwrites the online values with its full history, which slows down each lookup.
questions.why: The online store is read on the request path, so when the sync stops the old values keep being served silently and only freshness monitoring reveals it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only ever built a model from a single CSV file why we would adopt a feature store, and name one limit or tradeoff it adds.
lessons.modelAnswer: A feature store is where we define each input value once, such as a driver's average delivery time over seven days, and then serve that same value to both training and live predictions. Without one, the training job and the serving app often compute the same feature with different code, so the model sees different numbers in production than it learned from, and accuracy drops silently. The store keeps a historical offline copy for building training sets, using point-in-time lookups so future values do not leak into past examples, and a low-latency online copy keyed by entity ID for live requests. The tradeoff is operational cost: we now run pipelines that keep both copies fresh, the online store must scale with prediction traffic, and a stalled sync leaves stale values that still return successfully, so freshness needs monitoring.
rubricPoints: Defines a feature store as one shared place to define, compute, and serve features
Explains training-serving skew and how computing features once prevents it
Mentions the offline store for history and point-in-time lookups against leakage
Names a real tradeoff such as sync pipeline cost, online capacity, or stale values

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about where a feature's values come from and how they reach training and serving adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers feature stores.

lessons.plain: When a trained model is ready, the apps that want its predictions need a way to reach it. An endpoint is the network address that receives prediction requests and sends back answers. A public endpoint sits on the open internet, so any caller that has valid credentials can use it from almost anywhere. A private endpoint is reachable only from networks you connect to it, such as an isolated cloud network you control, so the traffic never crosses the open internet. Choosing between the two is mostly a question of who needs to call the model and from where.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants its internal billing system to call a fraud-scoring model without any of that traffic touching the public internet. Would you expose the model through a public endpoint, a private endpoint, or both, and why?
lessons.teach:
A deployed model is a trained model loaded onto managed serving machines so it can answer prediction requests. An endpoint is the network address that receives those requests and returns predictions. A public endpoint is reachable from the open internet, so any caller that can reach it and present valid credentials can use it. A private endpoint is reachable only from networks connected to it. A virtual private cloud (VPC) is an isolated network you control inside a cloud provider, and a peering connection is a private link between two such networks. Traffic to a private endpoint stays inside those linked networks. On Google Cloud's Vertex AI endpoints, the access mode is set when the endpoint is created, so it should be decided early in the design.

Why it works: the endpoint is a front door, and the access mode decides which routes can reach it. Public access relies on credentials and the service's own controls. Private access relies on network paths, so a caller must sit inside a network that has a connection to the endpoint's network.

Worked example: a mobile app calls a recommendation model. Step 1: the model is deployed to a public endpoint. Step 2: the app sends an HTTPS request with a credential. Step 3: the service checks the credential and returns predictions. Now a billing service inside the company network needs fraud scores without public exposure. Step 1: deploy to a private endpoint. Step 2: connect the billing network to the model's network with peering. Step 3: billing calls the private address and gets answers, while the internet has no route to it.

Common mistake: assuming a private endpoint is secure automatically, or that a public one is open to everyone by default. Both depend on configuration. A private endpoint with no connected caller simply fails for every client that cannot reach it.

Consequence: a misplaced endpoint in a running system shows up as connection failures and timeouts for the callers that lost their route, not as wrong predictions.

questions.prompt: Tallow Bay Insurance trains a claims-severity model and deploys it to a Vertex AI endpoint, the network address that receives prediction requests. The claims intake service runs in its own VPC (a virtual private cloud, an isolated network the company controls) and must not be reachable from the internet. Step 1: when the endpoint is created, the team sets its access mode to private, so the decision is made early. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the intake service calls the endpoint's private address and receives severity scores, while the internet has no route to the endpoint. Which missing step completes the design?
choices: The team attaches a public IP address to the endpoint so the intake service can reach it.
The team issues an API key to the intake service so the private endpoint can verify the service's identity.
The team switches the endpoint to public after creation so that every caller can reach it.
The team sets up a peering connection, a private link between two networks, between the intake VPC and the model's network so the intake service has a network path to the endpoint.
questions.why: Private access relies on network paths, so the caller's network must be connected to the endpoint's network, and peering is the link that does this.

questions.prompt: A partner logistics firm, outside your company's cloud network and with no network link to you, needs to call your freight-delay model over HTTPS using its own credentials. Which endpoint type fits?
choices: A private endpoint with a peering connection to the partner's on-premises network, because the partner cannot present credentials otherwise.
A public endpoint, because the partner can reach it over the internet and authenticate with its credential.
A private endpoint, because keeping any partner outside the network is always the safest choice.
A VPC with no endpoint at all, because the partner can read predictions straight from the model's storage bucket.
questions.why: A public endpoint is reachable from the internet and relies on credentials and the service's controls, while a private endpoint needs a network path the partner does not have.

questions.prompt: A team creates a private endpoint in their model network and peers it with only one of their six application networks. Services in the other five networks start failing. What do those five services most likely see?
choices: Predictions that are slightly less accurate, because the traffic is taking a longer route to the model.
Automatic fallback to a public endpoint serving the same model, so requests succeed with a delay.
Duplicate predictions, because the requests are being retried across several networks at once.
Connection failures or timeouts, because those networks have no route to the endpoint.
questions.why: A private endpoint is unreachable from networks without a connection, so callers in those networks fail to connect rather than receiving wrong predictions.

questions.prompt: A security reviewer says, 'The endpoint is private, so we can skip checking who calls it and through which networks.' Which response is most accurate?
choices: The reviewer is wrong: a private endpoint is only as safe as its configuration, including which networks are connected to it, so those connections still need review.
The reviewer is wrong because private endpoints cannot receive any requests at all, so nothing about callers needs checking here.
The reviewer is right only if the endpoint has no public IP and the model was trained without labels, since those two facts settle access.
The reviewer is right, because a private placement by itself removes any need to review who calls the endpoint and how they reach it.
questions.why: Both private and public endpoints depend on configuration, so a private endpoint is not secure automatically and its network connections must still be reviewed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a public model endpoint and a private model endpoint, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing a private endpoint.
lessons.modelAnswer: A public endpoint is reachable from the internet, so any client that has valid credentials can call the model from anywhere. Access control depends on the credentials and the service's own settings. A private endpoint is reachable only from networks connected to it, such as a VPC linked by peering, so traffic never crosses the open internet. The tradeoff is that every caller must have a network path to the endpoint. Mobile apps or partner systems outside that network cannot use it without extra connectivity work, and a missing or misconfigured link shows up as timeouts, not as clear errors. Private endpoints also do not remove the need for authentication. I would choose a public endpoint for broad external access and a private endpoint for internal services that must keep prediction traffic off the internet.
rubricPoints: Public endpoints are reachable from the internet and rely on credentials and service controls.
Private endpoints are reachable only from connected networks, so traffic stays off the open internet.
A private endpoint requires callers to have a network path, which adds setup and limits outside clients.
Private does not mean unauthenticated; access control still matters.

suggested.rationale: Choosing an endpoint access mode is mostly configuration and product fact, which is best learned by reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML endpoints.

lessons.plain: Serving hardware is the processor that runs a trained model when it answers requests, which is called inference. Choosing it means matching the processor to the model's work and to the speed, cost, and location you need. A CPU is a general-purpose chip that handles most small jobs well. A GPU is a chip with many simple workers that run lots of similar arithmetic at once. A TPU is Google's custom chip built for that kind of arithmetic. Edge means the model runs on a device near the user, such as a phone, a camera, or a vehicle, instead of in a data centre.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small model scores a row of 20 numbers from a spreadsheet, and a large model turns a photo into a label. Which one do you think gains more from a GPU, and why?
lessons.teach:
Serving hardware is the kind of processor that runs a trained model when it answers requests, which is called inference. Four families are common. A CPU (central processing unit) is a general-purpose processor with a few powerful cores. It handles small models, tree-based models such as gradient-boosted trees, and preprocessing well, and it is usually the cheapest and most flexible choice. A GPU (graphics processing unit) has thousands of simpler cores that perform many multiply-and-add operations in parallel, which suits neural networks built from large matrices. A TPU (tensor processing unit) is Google's custom accelerator for the same matrix work, and it pays off mainly for large models in supported frameworks. Edge hardware means running the model on the device itself, such as a phone, camera, or vehicle unit, so no network round trip is needed and the model can work offline.

The model's arithmetic decides the fit. Parallel hardware helps only when the work splits into many equal pieces, and the model's weights plus a batch of inputs must fit in the accelerator's memory.

Worked example. A fraud model is a gradient-boosted tree with 200 features that takes 5 ms per request on a CPU. Step 1: identify the model type. Trees gain little from a GPU. Step 2: check latency. 5 ms sits well inside a 100 ms budget. Step 3: choose CPU and scale by adding replicas. Contrast a 50-layer image classifier serving 2,000 requests per second. It does dense matrix work, so a GPU is the likely choice, and you then confirm its memory holds the weights and a batch.

Common mistake: choosing the most powerful accelerator by default. An idle GPU bills every hour, and a small model can run slower on a GPU because moving data to and from the chip adds overhead.

Consequence: if the model does not fit in accelerator memory, the replica fails at startup or crashes under a large batch, and autoscaling only creates more replicas that fail the same way.

questions.prompt: A retailer serves a 3-layer dense ranking network with about 40 MB of weights for its online store, and needs to handle 300 requests per second. Step 1: the network is mostly large matrix multiplications, so a GPU is a candidate. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the check passes, so the team chooses a GPU and adds replicas to meet the throughput target. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Move the model to an edge device, because edge hardware is always faster than a GPU.
Measure whether a TPU is cheaper, and choose it before checking anything else.
Confirm that the weights plus a batch of inputs fit in the accelerator's memory.
Skip the memory check, because a GPU is fast enough to hold any model.
questions.why: The teaching text says the weights plus a batch of inputs must fit in the accelerator's memory, so that check is the missing Step 2 before choosing the GPU and scaling replicas.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines edge hardware for model serving?
choices: A large cluster of CPUs in a data center that splits requests across many machines.
A custom Google accelerator built specifically for large matrix operations.
A GPU rented by the hour to run training jobs overnight.
Running the model on the device itself, such as a phone or camera, so no network round trip is needed and it can work offline.
questions.why: The teaching text defines edge hardware as running the model on the device itself, which removes the network round trip and allows offline operation.

questions.prompt: A team serves a gradient-boosted tree model with 80 features that takes 8 ms per request, against a 100 ms latency budget. Which serving choice fits the hardware guidance?
choices: Use a TPU, since TPUs are the most powerful option for every model type.
Move the model to a TPU and an edge device at the same time for redundancy.
Buy a GPU, since any model served in production should run on an accelerator.
Choose a CPU and scale by adding replicas, since trees gain little from a GPU and the latency budget is easily met.
questions.why: Tree-based models gain little from parallel accelerators, and 8 ms sits well inside the 100 ms budget, so a CPU with replicas is the appropriate choice.

questions.prompt: A team serves a neural network with 2 GB of weights on a GPU that has 4 GB of memory. Under load with batches of 32 inputs, the replicas crash. The team adds autoscaling so more replicas are created during peak traffic. What is the most likely result?
choices: The crashes stop, because more replicas spread the batch memory across machines.
Throughput improves, because the GPU moves data to the CPU and frees memory automatically.
The model switches to a CPU automatically, so the crashes disappear without any change.
The new replicas fail the same way, because each one must still hold the weights and a large batch in its own accelerator memory.
questions.why: Autoscaling only adds copies of the same serving setup, and if the model and batch do not fit in accelerator memory, every new replica crashes in the same way.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should not just serve every model on the largest GPU we can get. Explain how you would choose between CPU, GPU, TPU, and edge for one model, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the model type and the latency budget. A tree-based model with a few hundred features is mostly branching logic and small arithmetic, so a CPU is usually fast enough, and I can scale it by adding cheap replicas. A large neural network does big matrix multiplications, so a GPU or TPU can cut latency and raise throughput, but only if the weights and a batch fit in accelerator memory. Edge makes sense when the answer must come back without a network, or when data must stay on the device. The tradeoff with an accelerator is cost: an idle GPU still bills every hour, and a small model can run slower on it because of data transfer overhead. So I would benchmark two or three options at the expected request rate and pick the cheapest one that meets the latency target.
rubricPoints: Matches the processor to the model type, such as CPU for trees and GPU or TPU for large neural networks.
Checks latency and throughput targets before choosing hardware.
Confirms that model weights and batch size fit in accelerator memory.
Names a tradeoff, such as accelerator cost or idle time, or overhead on small models.
Mentions edge when offline use, privacy, or no network round trip is required.

suggested.rationale: Choosing hardware means reasoning through a scenario about model type, latency, and cost, which a short exam-style case teaches better than reading a catalogue.

lessons.plain: Scaling the serving backend means changing how many copies of a model are running and how they share incoming requests, so the service keeps up when traffic grows. Think of a checkout line in a shop. One till can only serve so many customers an hour, so when the queue gets long you open more tills, and you close some when it shrinks. Throughput is how many requests the system finishes per second. A good setup adds copies as load rises and removes them when it falls, without users waiting too long at any point. This lesson covers how to estimate how many copies you need, which signal tells the system to add or remove them, and why adding copies does not always fix a slow service.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model server handles 10 requests per second on one copy. Traffic rises to 50 requests per second, and each request takes the same time as before. Roughly how many copies do you think you need, and why might the real answer be somewhat more than the simple division gives?
lessons.teach:
A replica is one identical running copy of a model server. Concurrency is how many requests a single replica works on at the same moment. Latency is how long one request takes from start to finish. Throughput is how many requests complete per second. Little's law says the average number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average latency. Autoscaling is the system changing the replica count automatically based on a signal such as concurrent requests or CPU use. A minimum replica count keeps capacity warm, and a maximum caps cost. A utilization target is the busy level you aim for, leaving headroom for spikes.

Worked example: traffic is 200 requests per second and latency is 0.1 seconds. In-flight requests are 200 x 0.1 = 20. One replica safely handles 8 at once, so 20 / 8 = 2.5, which rounds up to 3 replicas. Aiming for 70 percent busy gives 8 x 0.7 = 5.6 usable slots per replica. Then 20 / 5.6 = 3.57, which rounds up to 4. If traffic doubles to 400 requests per second, in-flight requests reach 40, and 40 / 5.6 = 7.14, so you need 8.

Common mistake: assuming more replicas fixes every slowdown. If latency rises because a downstream database is slow, Little's law says in-flight requests pile up, so the autoscaler adds replicas that all call the same slow database and make it worse. In a running system, a scale-up that arrives late does nothing for requests that have already timed out, and a scale-from-zero setup adds a cold-start delay while a new copy loads the model.

A serving backend scales with throughput by matching the number of replicas to in-flight requests at a chosen busy level, and the bottleneck must be found before adding copies.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's route-scoring service receives 150 requests per second, and each request takes 0.2 seconds from start to finish. So the average number of requests in flight is 150 x 0.2 = 30. One replica can work on 6 requests at once, and the team wants each replica about 60 percent busy to leave room for spikes, so each replica gives 6 x 0.6 = 3.6 usable slots. Dividing 30 by 3.6 gives 8.33. Which replica count should the team set?
choices: 5, because the 60 percent target is dropped once the in-flight count is known
9, because a fractional replica must be rounded up to a whole one
8, because the result is rounded down to the nearest whole replica
10, because one spare replica is added on top of the rounded result
questions.why: Replicas are whole machines, and 8.33 needs headroom, so rounding up gives 9, which is the first whole count that covers the in-flight load at the chosen busy level.

questions.prompt: A search ranking service finishes 480 requests during a 30-second window. What is its throughput?
choices: 480 completed requests per second
0.0625 completed requests per second
30 completed requests per second
16 completed requests per second
questions.why: Throughput is completed requests divided by time, so 480 divided by 30 gives 16 requests per second.

questions.prompt: A payments API's latency rises from 0.1 seconds to 0.5 seconds because the database it calls has slowed down. Its traffic is unchanged, and the team's autoscaler starts adding replicas. What is the best next step?
choices: Keep adding replicas until latency returns to 0.1 seconds
Find the slow database as the bottleneck before adding more copies
Remove the minimum replica count so idle copies shut down
Lower the maximum replica count so cost stays fixed
questions.why: Longer latency at the same traffic means more requests are in flight, and extra replicas would send even more calls to the same slow database, so the bottleneck must be fixed first.

questions.prompt: A file-conversion service receives 40 requests per second, and each request takes 0.25 seconds from start to finish. What is the average number of requests in flight at any moment?
choices: 40 requests in flight
160 requests in flight
0.00625 requests in flight
10 requests in flight
questions.why: Little's law multiplies the arrival rate by the average latency, so 40 multiplied by 0.25 gives 10 requests in flight on average.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a model serving backend should scale as throughput grows. Say how you would decide the number of replicas, and name one limit or tradeoff of scaling on a single signal such as CPU.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the traffic rate and the average latency. Multiplying them gives the average number of requests in flight, because that is how many requests the service must hold at once. Divide that by how many requests one replica handles concurrently, adjusted to a target busy level like 70 percent so there is room for spikes. Round up, then set a minimum for steady traffic and a maximum for cost. For the autoscaling signal, I would use something close to load, such as concurrent requests, rather than only CPU. The tradeoff with CPU is that a model can be slow while the CPU looks idle, for example when it waits on a database or a GPU, so the autoscaler would not add copies when users are waiting. The other tradeoff is cold start: a new replica needs time to load the model, so scaling up early matters, and scaling to zero saves money but adds delay to the first request.
rubricPoints: Throughput times latency gives the average number of in-flight requests, which sets the required capacity.
Replica count comes from in-flight requests divided by per-replica concurrency, with headroom for a target busy level.
Scaling on a single signal such as CPU can miss slow waits on dependencies or accelerators.
Cold start delay and minimum replica settings affect how quickly the service responds to a spike.
Adding replicas does not fix a bottleneck in a shared downstream dependency.

suggested.rationale: The autoscale engine would let the learner set replica bounds and watch how a signal and a latency change drive scaling decisions, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Tuning a model means adjusting the settings that control how it learns during training and how it runs when it answers requests in production. Training settings, called hyperparameters, are choices you make before training starts, such as how fast the model learns or how many layers it has. Serving settings decide how many copies of the model run, how many requests each copy handles at once, and what hardware it uses. Good tuning balances accuracy, speed, and cost, and it is measured with real numbers rather than guessed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model scores well in testing but answers each request slowly when thousands of users arrive at once. Name one setting you could change during training and one setting you could change while serving, and say what each change would trade away.
lessons.teach: A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training starts, such as the learning rate (how big a step the model takes when correcting its mistakes), the number of trees or layers, or the batch size (how many examples are processed together). The model does not learn these from data; you search for good values. A hyperparameter tuning job runs many training trials with different combinations, scores each one on a validation set (data held back from training), and reports the best combination. Vertex AI offers this as a managed service, so the search runs on Google's infrastructure rather than your own machines.  Serving tuning is different. Once a model is deployed, the settings that matter are the number of replicas (identical copies of the model server), the minimum and maximum replica counts used by autoscaling, the number of requests each replica handles concurrently, and the machine type. Autoscaling adds replicas when load rises and removes them when load falls. Throughput is roughly replicas multiplied by the requests each replica can handle per second, so doubling replicas roughly doubles capacity until another bottleneck, such as a shared database, takes over.  Worked example: a fraud model answers in 300 ms per request on one replica that handles 4 requests at a time. That is about 13 requests per second per replica. Peak load is 100 requests per second, so you need at least 8 replicas, plus headroom. You set the maximum to 12 and the minimum to 2 so you pay for little capacity overnight.  Common mistake: tuning only for the best offline score and ignoring latency and cost, then discovering the most accurate model is too slow or too expensive to serve.  Consequence: if the minimum replica count is too low, a sudden spike forces new replicas to start while requests queue, and latency rises for every user until capacity catches up. Tuning for production means choosing the model and serving settings together, against measured latency and cost targets.

questions.prompt: A document-classification model on a logistics platform takes 500 ms to answer one request, and each replica can work on 2 requests at the same time. This is its concurrency, meaning how many requests one copy of the model server handles simultaneously. Peak load is 60 requests per second. Step 1, already done: throughput per replica = 2 ÷ 0.5 s = 4 requests per second. Step 2, already done: replicas needed at peak = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. Step 3, missing: add 20 percent headroom (spare capacity kept free for unexpected traffic) to the step 2 result and use that as the maximum replica count. What is the maximum replica count?
choices: 18 replicas
4 replicas
15 replicas
30 replicas
questions.why: Headroom of 20 percent applied to the 15 replicas needed at peak gives 15 × 1.2 = 18, so 18 is the maximum.

questions.prompt: In a model serving setup, what does the concurrency setting of a single replica mean?
choices: The number of requests one replica works on at the same moment
The total requests per second the whole service accepts
The number of training trials run in a tuning job
The number of identical model copies running in the group
questions.why: Concurrency is the number of requests one replica processes at the same time, which is separate from how many replicas exist.

questions.prompt: A translation model is served with a minimum of 1 replica. Traffic is quiet overnight, then jumps sharply at 9 am. What is the most likely effect on users during the first minutes of the jump?
choices: Answers become less accurate because the model retrains on the new traffic
Training hyperparameters are re-tuned automatically, slowing the answers
Latency rises for everyone while new replicas start and queued requests wait
The autoscaler removes replicas to save cost, so requests are rejected at once
questions.why: When the minimum is too low, a spike forces new replicas to start while requests queue, so latency rises for all users until capacity catches up.

questions.prompt: A team picked a fraud model because it had the best offline validation score, but in production each answer takes 1.5 seconds and the serving bill is high. Which earlier mistake best explains this?
choices: Starting the day with too few replicas
Using a validation set that was too small
Setting the learning rate too high during training
Tuning only for the offline score and ignoring latency and cost targets
questions.why: Choosing a model on offline accuracy alone, without measuring latency and cost, is the common mistake that leads to a model too slow or expensive to serve.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tune a model for production: what you would search over during training, what you would set for serving, and one limit or tradeoff that could make the most accurate model the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split tuning into two stages. During training, a managed hyperparameter tuning job runs several trials over settings like learning rate and batch size, scores each trial on held-out validation data, and keeps the best combination. I would not simply pick the highest score, because a model that wins by a small margin may be much slower to answer. For serving, I would measure latency and throughput under realistic load, then set the replica range and per-replica concurrency so peak traffic is covered with some headroom. The tradeoff is accuracy versus latency and cost. A larger model may improve the metric but need more replicas or bigger hardware, which raises the bill and can push response times past what users tolerate. So I would choose the model that meets the latency target at an acceptable cost, not the one with the top offline number.
rubricPoints: Training hyperparameters are set before training and searched through trials scored on validation data.
Serving settings include replica counts, autoscaling bounds, per-replica concurrency and machine type.
Throughput scales roughly with replicas times per-replica capacity, until a shared bottleneck limits it.
The best offline score is not automatically the right production choice because of latency and cost.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about tradeoffs between training and serving settings and explaining them back, which no listed mission or planned engine covers directly.

lessons.plain: Before a machine learning model is retrained and released automatically, the pipeline checks two things: whether the new data looks like the data the model expects, and whether the newly trained model is actually good enough to replace the one in use. These checks are called gates. If a check fails, the pipeline stops or keeps the old model, so a bad batch of data or a worse model never reaches the systems relying on its predictions. Think of a quality inspector on a production line who can stop the belt before a faulty product is boxed and shipped.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a model is retrained every night on fresh data, what could go wrong that a pipeline should catch before the new model goes live?
lessons.teach:
Validation here means automated checks that run inside a pipeline and decide whether it may continue. There are two kinds. Data validation checks incoming data against expectations: the columns and their types (called a schema), allowed value ranges, the share of missing values, and drift, meaning the statistics have shifted compared with the data the current model was trained on. Model validation checks a newly trained candidate: its score on a held-out test set (examples never used for training or tuning), its score on important slices such as one region or customer group, and its score compared with the model currently in production, called the baseline. A gate is a pipeline step that passes or fails based on such a rule.

Why it works: a pipeline runs without a person watching, so the only protection against bad inputs or regressions is a rule checked every time. Catching a problem before the model is promoted is far cheaper than finding it after customers see it.

Worked example: a nightly job retrains a delivery-time model. Step 1: the data gate reads the new batch and finds the distance column now holds text in 12 percent of rows, which breaks the expected numeric type, so the gate fails and training never starts. Step 2: the next night the data is clean and training produces a candidate with an average error of 4.1 minutes. Step 3: the model gate scores both the candidate and the production model on the same held-out set. The production model scores 3.6 minutes, so the candidate fails the rule that it must not be worse than the baseline, and the pipeline keeps the current model.

Common mistake: checking only one overall number, computed on data that was also used to tune the model. This hides leaked test data and weak performance on specific slices.

Consequence: without gates, a broken batch could silently promote a worse model to live traffic, and the damage may only surface as complaints days later. A pipeline should never promote a model that has not passed both its data checks and its comparison against the current model.

questions.prompt: A coffee chain retrains a daily model that forecasts how many cups each store will sell. Each night a pipeline runs two checks before it can continue. Step 1, the data gate: the new sales batch stores cups_sold as whole numbers, as expected, and 1.5 percent of rows are missing a value against a limit of 5 percent, so the gate passes. Step 2, training: a candidate model is trained on the same training window and scored on a held-out set (examples never used for training or tuning) drawn from the last four weeks, with an average error of 6.2 cups per store per day. Step 3 is the promotion decision, and it is the step still missing from the pipeline notes: the team must decide what the model gate has to check before the candidate can replace the live model. Which rule completes step 3 correctly?
choices: Score the candidate on the four weeks it was trained on, since that is where it will look strongest, and promote if it passes
Score the live production model on the same held-out four weeks, and promote the candidate only if its error is not worse than that baseline
Add the four held-out weeks to the training data, retrain, and promote whatever the new model reports on those same weeks
Promote the candidate because 6.2 cups is under the fixed limit of 10 cups the team set last year, without looking at the live model
questions.why: The gate must compare the candidate with the production model (the baseline) on the same held-out data, because a fixed limit alone cannot show whether the candidate is an improvement.

questions.prompt: In a pipeline, which of these is a data validation check rather than a model validation check?
choices: Comparing a new candidate's error with the error of the model currently in production
Measuring a candidate's error separately for customers in one city
Confirming that a price column holds decimal numbers and that no more than 5 percent of its rows are empty
Scoring a candidate on a test set that it was never trained on
questions.why: Data validation checks incoming data against expectations such as types, value ranges and missing-value share, while the other three examine a trained candidate model.

questions.prompt: A team repeatedly adjusts the settings of a churn model while watching one overall accuracy number computed on the same test set they tune against, then reports that number as the result. What is the main risk?
choices: The data gate will reject every batch that arrives after the tuning run
The model will be too large to store in a cache
The reported number may be inflated, since the test data influenced tuning, and weak results for specific groups stay hidden
The baseline model will be retired automatically the next morning
questions.why: Tuning on the test set leaks it into the decisions, so the single overall number overstates quality and can hide poor performance on important slices.
