suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a production scenario that shows which signal catches which kind of drift or skew adds the most here, since no listed mission or planned engine covers ML monitoring directly.

lessons.plain: Imagine hiring a writer whose answers you cannot predict word for word. You cannot check them with a simple right-or-wrong test, so you need a way to judge quality, test changes before they go live, and keep watching after launch. That is what evaluating and monitoring a generative AI system means. A generative model is one that writes new text, images or code. You prepare a set of sample questions and what good answers look like, run the system against them whenever something changes, and sample real conversations once it is live to catch answers that are off-topic, unsupported by your documents, or unsafe. The goal is to notice quality slipping before your users do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team swaps their chatbot to a newer model and the demo answers look better. Why might that still be a bad release, and how would you check before shipping?
lessons.teach: Generative AI evaluation means measuring whether a model's text, image or code output is good enough, and continuing that measurement after launch. A generative model can produce many acceptable answers to the same question, so there is no single right label to compare against. Instead you score outputs against criteria: relevance to the question, groundedness (whether the answer is supported by the source documents the system was given), safety, and format. A golden dataset is a fixed set of representative prompts paired with reference answers or scoring rubrics, kept unchanged so that scores can be compared over time. An LLM-as-judge is a second model prompted with your rubric to score outputs; it is cheap and scalable, but its scores must be checked against human ratings. Evaluation works in three layers. Offline evaluation runs the golden dataset before release. Regression testing reruns the same set whenever the prompt, model version or retrieval settings change, and compares against the previous baseline. Online monitoring samples real production traffic, scores it with the same rubric, and alerts when a trend moves. Worked example: a support bot answers from a policy document. The golden set has 200 questions. A candidate model raises relevance from 91 percent to 94 percent but drops groundedness from 96 percent to 85 percent. Tracing the failures shows 30 answers citing policy text absent from the retrieved passages. The release is blocked, because the groundedness loss outweighs the relevance gain. Common mistake: judging a change from a few demos, or from one overall average with no fixed dataset and no human check, so you cannot tell whether things improved or got worse. Consequence: without online sampling, a silent model update or a shift in user questions can produce confident wrong answers for weeks before anyone notices. Evaluation is how a team knows that a generative system is still doing its job after every change.

questions.prompt: A fintech team builds a code-writing assistant for its engineers. An LLM-as-judge is a second language model prompted with a scoring rubric to grade another model's outputs. The team keeps a golden dataset, meaning a fixed set of 120 coding tasks graded with the same rubric every time, so scores stay comparable. Step 1: the current model's outputs are graded by the judge, and 81 percent pass the safety and format rubric. Step 2: a new model version is graded by the same judge on the same 120 tasks, and 89 percent pass. Step 3: the team writes the release note with the 89 percent figure. The team has not yet done the one check that shows whether the judge's grades agree with people's grades. What should happen next, before the 89 percent is trusted?
choices: Enlarge the golden dataset to 1,000 tasks so the average is more precise.
Have people rate a sample of the same outputs and measure how often the judge agrees with them.
Ask the model vendor to publish its own safety score for the new version.
Rerun the judge on the same 120 tasks a second time to confirm the 89 percent is repeatable.
questions.why: An LLM-as-judge is cheap but its scores must be checked against human ratings, and comparing the judge with a human sample is the step that shows whether its grades can be trusted.

questions.prompt: In generative AI evaluation, what is the main purpose of a golden dataset?
choices: To provide a fixed set of prompts with reference answers or rubrics that stays unchanged, so scores can be compared over time.
To serve as the training data used to fine-tune the model before it is released.
To let each release team pick its own favourite examples so the test feels relevant to that release.
To hold the newest real user questions from production, refreshed each week so the test reflects current traffic.
questions.why: A golden dataset is kept fixed and unchanged so that scores from different model versions or dates can be compared fairly.

questions.prompt: A hospital's internal policy assistant is about to have its retrieval settings changed, which decides which document passages are passed to the model. Which evaluation layer should check that the change has not hurt answers, and how?
choices: Online monitoring only, watching live traffic after the change goes out and waiting for an alert.
Training a new model from scratch on the hospital's documents so that retrieval no longer matters.
Regression testing, rerunning the same fixed set of questions and comparing the results against the previous baseline.
A single demo session where a manager asks three questions and approves the change if they look fine.
questions.why: Regression testing reruns the same fixed set whenever retrieval, prompt or model version changes and compares against the prior baseline, which shows whether anything got worse.

questions.prompt: A team reports that its LLM judge gives their product's answers an average score of 92 percent every week. The question set is rotated each week, and no person has ever checked the judge's grades. What is the core problem with this report?
choices: With no fixed dataset and no human check, the team cannot tell whether a change improved or worsened the answers.
Scores above 90 percent are always reliable, so the team has nothing to worry about.
The weekly average should be replaced with the single best answer from each week.
The judge should be replaced with a human reviewer, because any model-based scoring is always wrong.
questions.why: Without a fixed golden dataset and a check against human ratings, a single overall average cannot show whether quality really moved, which is the common mistake this objective warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a new model version of our support bot is safe to ship, and name one limit of the method you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not decide from a few demo answers. First I would rerun our fixed golden set, a few hundred representative questions with reference answers or a scoring rubric, against both the current and the new model, and compare scores on relevance, groundedness to the policy documents, safety and format. Because outputs vary, I would have people rate a sample, and if we use an LLM judge I would check its scores against those human ratings first. Then I would look at each category separately rather than one average, since a gain in relevance can hide a drop in groundedness. The limit is that the golden set only covers the questions we thought of, and judge scores are approximations. So after release I would sample live traffic with the same rubric and watch the trend, rather than treating the pre-release result as proof.
rubricPoints: Uses a fixed golden dataset with the same rubric for both model versions so results are comparable
Checks an LLM judge against human ratings before trusting its scores
Breaks results down by criterion such as groundedness, not one overall average
Names a real limit, such as coverage of the test set or approximate judge scores, and pairs it with production monitoring

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a release decision in a production scenario adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine directly targets generative AI evaluation.

scenarios.title: Tidewater Pantry weekly demand and document intake
scenarios.scenario:
Tidewater Pantry Co. is a fictional regional grocery distributor with 40 stores. Its analytics team has three years of weekly unit sales per store and product in BigQuery, a Google Cloud data warehouse that stores tables and runs SQL over them. The team has three requests. First, operations wants an eight-week forecast of unit sales for each store and product so that trucks are loaded correctly. Second, the purchasing clerks scan supplier invoices as PDFs and want the invoice total and supplier name pulled out automatically. Third, the marketing group wants short product descriptions drafted from a spreadsheet of ingredients and sizes, reviewed by a person before publishing. The lead engineer, who is new to ML, has asked you to plan the work. Answer the following:

1. For the demand forecast, decide whether a low-code model built in BigQuery ML or AutoML is the right fit, or whether a foundation model such as Gemini should be used. Give one reason for your choice and say what the model is predicting.

2. Describe the steps you would take inside BigQuery ML to prepare features for the forecast (for example a promotion flag and a local holiday flag), train the model on the historical table, and then generate predictions for the next eight weeks. Name one feature you would select or drop and explain why.

3. For the invoice totals and the product descriptions, name the industry-specific service you would use for the invoices and explain why it fits better than a general model. For the descriptions, explain which Gemini-based approach fits and name one thing you would do to control cost or latency for that application.
subParts: Choose the model approach for the forecast
Prepare features, train, and predict in BigQuery ML
Match services to invoices and descriptions, and control Gemini cost
modelAnswer: Use a low-code model in BigQuery ML, specifically a time-series forecasting model, because the problem is predicting a number (unit sales) over future weeks from a large table of past numbers that already lives in BigQuery. Low-code means you build the model with SQL statements rather than writing a full training program. Forecasting is a kind of regression over time: the model learns how sales change week to week and season to season. A foundation model such as Gemini is a large general model trained on huge amounts of text and images; it is not the efficient or measurable choice for predicting a numeric series from a clean table, and it would be harder to evaluate. The justification should name the target as weekly unit sales per store and product.

Start by building a training table in SQL that has one row per store, product and week, with the sales value as the target and columns such as a promotion flag (1 if a promotion ran that week) and a local holiday flag. Next, train a forecasting model in BigQuery ML pointing at that table, telling it which column is the time column, which is the value to forecast, and which columns identify each series (store and product). Then run the prediction function in BigQuery ML with a horizon of eight weeks to produce the forecast rows. For feature selection, keep the promotion and holiday flags because they explain known spikes, and drop an identifier-like column such as an internal row ID, because it carries no real signal and can cause the model to memorise rows rather than learn patterns. Explain the choice in one sentence.

For the supplier invoices, use Document AI, a managed service that reads scanned documents and extracts named fields such as supplier name and total amount. It fits better than a general model because it is built for invoices and forms, returns structured fields, and needs little or no custom training for common layouts. For the product descriptions, a Gemini model used through its API is the right kind of tool, because the task is open-ended text generation, and a human reviews the output before publishing. To control cost or latency, pick a smaller or lower-cost Gemini model variant if quality is adequate, limit the length of the output, or cache repeated requests. Name one of these and state the trade-off, such as lower quality or fewer words in exchange for lower cost and faster replies.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Mobility: Preparing Trip and Support Data for a Shared Demand Model
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Mobility is a fictional e-scooter rental company with a small machine learning team in three cities. The team wants a model that predicts how many scooters each station will need on a given evening, and a second prototype that summarizes customer support tickets. The raw inputs are a tabular export of about 40 GB of daily trip logs, stored in a data warehouse, plus several hundred thousand free-text support tickets and a folder of scanned damage photos. Some of the ticket and trip records include rider names, phone numbers, and payment-card last-four digits, which counts as personally identifiable information (PII), meaning any data that could identify a person either directly or when combined with other fields. The team uses hosted Jupyter-style notebooks, meaning browser-based notebook environments run by Google Cloud, so that engineers can share work. A feature store is a managed catalog where computed input values, called features, are saved once and reused by both training jobs and the live prediction service. Training-serving skew is the problem that occurs when the values used to train a model are calculated differently from the values the live service sees, which quietly lowers accuracy in production. Your manager asks you to handle the following, and each part is graded separately.

1. The trip logs need a daily aggregation step (counting trips per station per hour) that must run on the full 40 GB every night. Choose a tool for that step from BigQuery (a serverless SQL warehouse that runs queries over very large tables), Dataflow (a managed service that runs batch or streaming data pipelines), Apache Spark (a distributed engine for large data processing), or in-memory Python with pandas (a single-machine library that loads data into RAM), and justify your choice in terms of scale and complexity.

2. Before the notebook team can see any ticket text, the PII must be removed or masked. Describe the steps you would take, and explain where the station-level demand features should be stored so that the training notebook and the live prediction service read the same values.

3. The support-ticket summarizer is a generative model. Name the experiment environment you would use to record runs, parameters, and metrics so that versions and lineage (the recorded history of which data, code, and model produced each result) can be compared later. Then propose one evaluation method for summary quality, including whether LLM-as-a-judge (using a second language model to score the first model's outputs against a rubric) is appropriate and what its main limitation is.
subParts: Choose and justify the preprocessing tool for the nightly trip aggregation
Describe PII handling and where to store shared demand features
Pick an experiment-tracking environment and an evaluation method for the summarizer
modelAnswer: BigQuery is the strongest fit. The trip logs are tabular, already live in a warehouse, and the job is a grouped count per station per hour, which is a standard SQL aggregation that BigQuery runs in parallel without the team managing servers. Dataflow would also work at this scale but adds pipeline code the team does not need for a simple nightly count. Spark requires cluster management, and pandas on one machine would likely run out of memory with 40 GB, so it is the weakest choice here.

Remove or mask PII before data reaches shared notebooks: drop names and phone numbers entirely when the model does not need them, replace any needed identifier with a salted hash or a random token, and reduce card data to nothing beyond what is necessary. Restrict who can read the raw tables, and keep the masked copy as the only version the team uses. Store the station-level demand features (such as trips per station per hour and rolling seven-day averages) in the feature store, computed once by the shared pipeline. Training and the live service then both read the same stored values, which prevents training-serving skew. A common mistake is computing the feature differently in the notebook than in the service, so accuracy looks good in testing and drops after launch.

Record the summarizer's runs in Vertex AI Experiments, which tracks parameters, metrics, and the data and model artifacts used for each run, so versions and lineage can be compared side by side. For evaluation, use a fixed set of human-written reference summaries and score the model on how faithful and complete its summaries are, using a rubric. LLM-as-a-judge can be used to scale this scoring, but it is appropriate only after the judge has been checked against human ratings on a sample, because the judge model can have its own biases, such as favoring longer answers or its own writing style, and those biases would silently distort the comparison.

scenarios.title: Brindle Freight: Scaling a Warehouse Staffing Forecast
scenarios.scenario:
Brindle Freight Co. is a fictional parcel company with 14 regional sorting warehouses. Its operations team wants a model that predicts next-day package volume for each warehouse so managers can schedule shifts. A prototype built by an analyst in BigQuery, Google's data warehouse, works on a three-year table of daily volumes, weather, holidays, and promotion flags. The prototype is not ready for production. Three constraints apply. First, the labor planning committee requires that every forecast can be explained to a manager in plain terms, because staffing cuts based on an unexplained number have caused disputes before. Second, the schedule is published each night, so a batch of forecasts for all 14 warehouses must finish in under 30 minutes, with no need for real-time answers. Third, the team has a small budget and no in-house deep learning specialist. Work through the following:

1. Choose the model type and the product you would use to train this forecast, and explain why your choice satisfies the explainability requirement and the nightly batch constraint.

2. Decide whether this training job needs a CPU, GPU, or TPU, and explain your choice. Then say what would change your answer if the team later added a text model that reads free-form driver notes.

3. The first full training run on a deep neural network fails partway through with an out-of-memory error, and the team suspects the hyperparameters. Name the hyperparameters you would check first, explain what each controls, and say whether you would tune them or switch approach.
subParts: Model type and product choice with explainability and batch timing
Hardware choice for tabular training, and what changes for a text model
Diagnosing the failed deep neural network run and hyperparameter triage
modelAnswer: Use a tabular-friendly model rather than a deep neural network or a large language model. A DNN (deep neural network, a model made of many stacked layers of weighted calculations) and an LLM (large language model, a very large model trained on text) are powerful but hard to explain and expensive to run. ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average, a classical statistical model for a single time series that predicts from its own past values and differences) is interpretable but handles one series at a time and extra inputs like weather and promotions poorly, so it is a weak fit for 14 warehouses with many drivers. The better fit is a boosted tree or linear model on tabular data, trained with BigQuery ML (a feature of BigQuery that lets you create and train models using SQL, keeping the data where it already sits). Tree-based models can report which features drove each prediction, which supports the explanation requirement. Training and batch prediction run inside the warehouse, which fits the nightly 30-minute window and avoids moving data. Agent Platform AutoML (Google's managed service that searches model options for you) is also acceptable for tabular data, but BigQuery ML keeps the work simpler and cheaper here. Agent Platform Pipelines (a managed way to chain data preparation, training, and prediction steps into a repeatable workflow) would only be added later to automate the nightly run. A common mistake is choosing the most powerful model by default; the consequence here is a forecast nobody can defend in the committee and a nightly job that runs too long.

For this tabular job, a CPU (central processing unit, the general-purpose processor) is the right default. Gradient-boosted trees and linear models on a few hundred thousand rows are not dominated by the matrix arithmetic that GPUs (graphics processing units, chips built for parallel arithmetic) and TPUs (tensor processing units, Google's accelerator chips built for large neural network math) speed up. Adding an accelerator here adds cost and setup work without shortening the 30-minute window. If the team later adds a text model that reads driver notes, the answer changes: a transformer or other neural text model benefits from a GPU, and a very large text model with many training steps could justify a TPU, especially if the job is split across multiple accelerators using data parallelism (copying the model to each device and splitting the training batches among them) or model parallelism (splitting one large model across devices). Even then, the explainability requirement would need a separate, more interpretable model for the staffing forecast itself. A common mistake is assuming accelerators always make training faster; the consequence is paying for idle expensive hardware while the job is bottlenecked on reading data.

The most likely cause is that the batch size (the number of examples processed together in one training step) is too large for the memory on the device, and the number of layers or neurons (the width and depth of the network) may also be too high for this data size. Check batch size first, because reducing it usually fixes memory errors with the least side effects. Next check the learning rate (how far each training step moves the weights), which affects whether training converges, and the number of layers and units, which affects both memory and overfitting. Tuning means running a controlled search over these values, such as a few candidate batch sizes and learning rates, and keeping the best on validation data. Switching approach is the better call here, because the forecast needs explainability and a tabular tree model already meets the batch window. A deep neural network is a poor fit for this objective, so tuning its memory settings would spend time on the wrong model. Fine-tuning a pretrained foundation model, which adapts an already trained large model, is warranted only when a pretrained model is needed for a task like text. A common mistake is tuning hyperparameters on a model that is wrong for the constraint; the consequence is a longer project with a forecast still too opaque to publish.

scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern delivery-time model rollout
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional company that runs a grocery delivery service. Its data team has trained a delivery-time model, an XGBoost model, which is a tree-based model that predicts minutes until an order arrives. The model is registered in the Model Registry, the catalog where each trained model and its numbered versions are stored so teams can find and track them. Two products need predictions. First, the checkout page shows an estimated arrival time while a customer is still shopping, so each prediction must come back in well under a second. This is online inference, meaning a single request gets an immediate answer from a model that is always running behind an endpoint, which is a web address that accepts requests and returns predictions. Second, every night at 2 a.m., the warehouse planning system needs predictions for roughly 400,000 orders for the next day. Nobody is waiting on any single answer, so this is batch inference, meaning a large job that scores many records at once and writes results to storage. A new version of the model, version 2, was trained with an extra weather feature. The team wants to release it carefully, sending only a small share of live checkout traffic to it first and comparing its results with version 1 before a full switch. The platform is managed, so the team does not run its own servers. Complete the following three tasks. 1. Choose the deployment style for the checkout page and for the nightly job, and name one reason for each choice. 2. Describe how you would release version 2 using a canary deployment, which is a rollout where a small percentage of live traffic goes to the new version while the rest stays on the old one, and state what you would compare before increasing the share. 3. The checkout traffic spikes at dinner time. Explain how the serving backend adds or removes running copies of the model, called replicas, as request volume changes, and name one setting you would review so that the endpoint keeps up without paying for idle capacity all day.
subParts: Choose the deployment style for checkout and for the nightly job, with one reason each.
Describe a canary rollout of version 2 with a traffic split, and what you compare before increasing traffic.
Explain how replicas scale with request volume and name one scaling setting to review.
modelAnswer: Checkout needs online inference on a managed endpoint because a customer is waiting for each answer in real time and the page makes individual requests. The nightly job should use batch inference because it scores about 400,000 orders in one large run, nobody waits on a single result, and the output can be written to storage for the warehouse system to read the next morning. A good answer names both choices and gives a reason tied to latency for checkout and volume or cost for the batch job.

Deploy version 2 to the same endpoint as version 1 but give it a small traffic share, for example 5 percent, with the remaining 95 percent still on version 1. Before increasing the share, compare the two versions on the same live traffic: prediction latency, error rate, and accuracy of predicted arrival times against actual delivery times once they are known. Also check that the weather feature is available at serving time, not only in training data. If version 2 is no worse on these measures, raise the share in steps, and keep version 1 available so traffic can be moved back quickly if problems appear. A strong answer also notes that a canary rollout checks that the new version is safe to run, while an A/B test is a planned comparison of two versions to measure which performs better.

The serving backend runs one or more replicas, which are identical running copies of the model. When request volume rises, the platform adds replicas, and when it falls, it removes them, so capacity follows the load. The scaling is driven by settings such as the minimum and maximum number of replicas and a target metric, for example a target level of requests per replica or CPU use. A good review setting is the minimum replica count: too low and the first dinner-time requests may wait while new replicas start, too high and the team pays for idle copies overnight. A strong answer explains that adding replicas increases total throughput, meaning how many predictions per second the endpoint can handle, and names the trade-off between speed and cost.

scenarios.title: Keeping a weekly demand forecast current at a fictional grocery chain
scenarios.scenario:
Lumen Pantry Co. is a fictional grocery chain with 300 stores. Its data science team runs a demand forecast model that predicts how many units of each product each store will sell in the coming week. Store managers use these forecasts to order stock. Over the last two months, forecast error has grown, especially after the company changed its holiday promotion calendar. The team wants the model to stay current without someone manually retraining it each time. Some terms first. A retraining policy is the written rule that says when a model gets retrained and on what data. Continuous integration (CI) means automatically testing code and pipeline changes whenever they are committed. Continuous delivery (CD) means automatically packaging and releasing a validated model to an environment. Continuous training (CT) means the pipeline itself retrains the model on a schedule or when a trigger fires. Data validation means automatically checking that incoming data has the expected columns, types, ranges and distributions before it is used. Model validation means automatically checking that a newly trained model meets quality thresholds before it can be promoted. Training-serving skew means the features a model sees in production differ from the features it was trained on, usually because preprocessing was done differently in the two places. The team builds its pipeline on Agent Platform Pipelines, a managed service that runs a series of containerised steps in order, where each step's outputs feed the next. Your manager, Priya, asks you to take the first design pass. Answer the three sub-tasks below.

1. Propose a retraining policy for this forecast model. Say whether retraining should run on a fixed schedule, when a monitored signal crosses a threshold, or both, and justify your choice using the promotion calendar change as the example.

2. Describe where data validation and model validation sit in the pipeline, and state what should happen to a candidate model that fails model validation.

3. Explain how the team can make sure the preprocessing applied to store sales data during training is identical to the preprocessing applied when the forecast is served, and say what goes wrong if it is not.
subParts: Placement of data and model validation gates
modelAnswer: A sound answer combines a scheduled retrain, such as weekly, so the model always sees recent sales, with a trigger-based retrain that fires when monitored signals cross a threshold, such as forecast error rising above an agreed level or a shift in input distributions after a calendar change. The promotion calendar change is the example: a fixed weekly schedule would only pick up the new promotions after a delay, so a trigger on rising error or on a detected change in promotion-related inputs would start retraining sooner. A good answer also says the policy must name the trigger, the training window, and who approves promotion. The common mistake is choosing only a fixed schedule with no way to react, or retraining on every new data point without thresholds, which wastes compute and can chase noise.

Data validation sits at the start of the pipeline, before any training step, and checks schema, value ranges, missing values and distribution shift in the new sales data. Model validation sits after training and before the model is registered or deployed, and compares the candidate against the currently serving model on a held-out recent period, using agreed metrics and thresholds. If a candidate fails model validation, the pipeline must stop the promotion, keep the current serving model in place, record the failed run and its metrics, and alert the team. The common mistake is letting a failing candidate overwrite the production model, or running validation only manually after deployment. In a running system this matters because a bad forecast silently drives wrong store orders.

The team should put all preprocessing logic, such as scaling, encoding product and store identifiers, filling missing sales values and building lag features, into one shared transformation component or library that both the training pipeline step and the serving path call, and save the fitted transformation parameters with the model version so serving uses the exact same values learned during training. Using the same code path, and not rewriting the logic separately for the online service, is what keeps the two identical. If the two differ, for example if serving computes a rolling average over a different window or uses a newer category mapping, the model receives inputs it was never trained on, and forecast quality drops even though the model file has not changed. A common mistake is saving only the model weights and not the preprocessing parameters, so the serving side guesses them.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Claims Assistant: Leaks, Skew and Drift
scenarios.scenario: Harbourline Insurance is a fictional mid-size insurer that runs two production AI systems. The first is a generative claims assistant, built on a large language model (LLM, a text model that writes replies from a prompt). Adjusters paste claim notes into it for summaries, and some notes contain customers' national ID numbers and bank account numbers. The second is a tabular fraud model, which predicts from rows of numeric and category columns and sits behind an online endpoint that returns a score within a second of each request. Three weeks ago the data engineering team changed how the serving path computes the claim_amount feature. It now reports cents instead of dollars, while the training data still uses dollars. Since then the fraud-review rate has dropped sharply, and the security lead has asked for a review of the assistant's logs. Answer the following. 1. Choose the control that should stop account and ID numbers from reaching the LLM prompt and from appearing in its replies, and explain why one tool fits better than the alternatives. 2. Name the monitoring problem behind the fraud-score drop, say whether it is training-serving skew, data drift or concept drift, and explain how you would confirm it. 3. The security lead asks how you would notice if the fraud model began relying on a different set of features even though its input values still look normal. Explain the signal and how you would set up its monitoring.
modelAnswer: A regex is a pattern-matching rule that finds text of a given shape, such as nine digits in a row. It is cheap and fast and suits fixed formats, but it misses paraphrased or split data and cannot detect instructions hidden in a prompt. A safety filter scores content against harm categories such as hate or violence; it is the wrong fit for account data or prompt injection, which is an attempt to override the model's instructions through user text. Model Armor is a managed service that screens prompts and responses against configurable templates covering sensitive data, prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, and policy categories. The best answer is Model Armor placed in front of the LLM on both the input and the output, with regex kept as a cheap extra check for exact number formats. A common mistake is choosing regex alone or treating a harm filter as leak protection. The consequence of getting this wrong is that a reply echoing a bank account number gets stored in logs and seen by staff outside their authorised roles.

Training-serving skew is a gap between the feature values a model saw in training and the values it receives in production, usually because the two pipelines compute the same feature differently. Here the claim_amount unit changed from dollars to cents, so the live values are 100 times larger than the training values. The world did not change; the pipeline did. That makes this skew, not data drift, which is a change in the input distribution over time, and not concept drift, which is a change in the relationship between inputs and the correct answer. To confirm it, take a sample of claim IDs, compare the logged serving values for claim_amount against the stored training values for the same claims, and check the ratio. A ratio near 100 confirms the unit mismatch. A common mistake is retraining on the new data, which bakes the bug into the model. The consequence is that inflated amounts push scores away from what the model learned, so fraud cases slip through unreviewed.

Feature attribution drift is a change over time in how much each input feature contributes to predictions. Attributions are per-prediction scores, produced by explainability methods, that estimate how strongly each feature pushed a prediction up or down. Inputs can stay within their normal ranges while the model starts leaning on different features, which can signal a broken upstream feature or a shifted population. To set this up, log attribution values for a sample of predictions, compute the average attribution per feature over a rolling window, compare that against a baseline taken from the validation period, and alert when the ranking or size of the top features moves beyond a set threshold. A common mistake is monitoring only input value ranges, which misses this shift entirely. The consequence is silent degradation: the model keeps returning scores with no visible error while its decisions quietly change.
